name: Medical and Biological Chemistry
description: Complete study manual · 15 practical and laboratory class topics

topics.title: Introduction to medical chemistry. Chemistry and the environment. Chemistry of biogenic elements

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of medical chemistry and the stages of studying it, the mathematical skills needed for chemical calculations, chemical pollution of the environment and its effect on health, the rules of work in a chemical laboratory, and the properties, biological significance and qualitative reactions of s-, p- and d-elements.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the subject and tasks of medical chemistry and its links with other medical sciences;
the concepts of the mole, molar mass, mass fraction and concentration;
the main chemical pollutants of the environment and their effects on the body;
the classification of biogenic elements (macro-, micro- and ultramicroelements);
the physical and chemical properties and biological significance of s-, p- and d-elements;
the qualitative reactions of important cations and anions.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: follow the safety rules of a chemical laboratory and give first aid;
do simple calculations with moles, mass and concentration;
identify ions of biogenic elements with qualitative reactions;
solve situational problems and explain the chemical basis of an element deficiency or excess.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: About 97 % of body mass is made up of the **organogenic** elements — C, H, O, N, P, S. Macroelements make up more than 10^−2^ % of the body, microelements 10^−3^–10^−5^ %, and ultramicroelements less than 10^−5^ %.

summary.text: Flame colors: **“Sodium — a yellow sun, Potassium — a violet night, Calcium — a brick wall, Copper — a green leaf”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When diluting an acid, pour the **acid into the water**, never the reverse: if water is poured into concentrated H~2~SO~4~, the heat released boils the water instantly and the acid spatters.

sections.title: 1. The subject of medical chemistry and how to study it

blocks.text: **Medical chemistry** is the science that studies the laws of the chemical and physicochemical processes in a living organism, the properties of the substances that enter the body (food, drugs, poisons) and the methods used to analyze them. It brings together the parts of general, inorganic, physical and colloid, analytical and bioorganic chemistry that medicine needs, and it is the foundation for **biochemistry, normal physiology, pharmacology, hygiene and clinical laboratory diagnostics**.

For example, to understand the acid–base status of the blood (pH 7.35–7.45) one needs buffer systems; to understand water–electrolyte metabolism one needs solutions and osmosis; to understand how drugs act one needs the structure of organic compounds.
Stages of studying the subject

items: **Theory** — learn terms, definitions and laws by understanding their logic, not by rote.
**Formulas and equations** — write and balance reaction equations correctly.
**Calculation** — consolidate knowledge quantitatively by solving problems.
**Experiment** — check the theory with your own eyes in laboratory work.
**Medical interpretation** — link the result to the state of the body.

blocks.text: The calculations use **decimal logarithms** (pH, pK), **powers of ten** (10^−7^ mol/L), **proportions** and **unit conversions** (mL → L, mg → g, mmol → mol) most often. Checking the units at the end of every calculation prevents half of all mistakes.

parts.text: 1 mole of any substance contains 6.022·10^23^ particles. At standard conditions (0 °C, 101.3 kPa) 1 mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L.

blocks.text: The human body constantly exchanges matter with the environment: any chemical that enters with air, water or food eventually reaches the tissues. Substances released into the environment in amounts far above the natural cycle and harmful to living organisms are called **ecotoxicants**.

blocks.text: **Global problems:** the rise of CO~2~ and CH~4~ — the greenhouse effect; chlorofluorocarbons (freons) — destruction of the ozone layer and stronger ultraviolet radiation; the reaction of SO~2~ and NO~x~ with water — **acid rain** (pH < 5.6).

Dust made of salt and pesticide residues blown from the dried seabed has increased respiratory diseases, anemia, and kidney and liver diseases in Karakalpakstan and Khorezm. The high mineral content of drinking water promotes kidney stone formation.

sections.title: 3. Rules of work in a chemical laboratory

items: Work in the laboratory only in a lab coat; wear safety goggles and gloves when needed.
Eating, drinking and tasting reagents at the workplace are strictly forbidden.
Smell a substance without bending over the vessel: waft the air toward yourself with your hand.
When heating a test tube, never point its mouth at yourself or at a neighbor.
Work with volatile, toxic and odorous substances only in a **fume hood**.
When diluting concentrated acids, pour the **acid in a thin stream into the water**.
Draw a solution into a pipette with a **rubber bulb** (pipette filler), never by mouth.
Do not use flammable liquids (ether, alcohol, acetone) near an open flame.
After work, return the reagents to their places, clean the workplace and wash your hands.

blocks.text: Elements that are part of the body and perform a definite function in vital processes are called **biogenic elements**. V.I. Vernadsky showed that the elemental composition of the body reflects that of the Earth’s crust, yet living organisms accumulate some elements (C, N, P, I) thousands of times more than their surroundings.

blocks.text: Most of the body mass is made up of **oxygen (≈ 62 %)**, **carbon (≈ 21 %)**, **hydrogen (≈ 10 %)**, **nitrogen (≈ 3 %)**, **calcium (≈ 2 %)** and **phosphorus (≈ 1 %)**.

blocks.text: The biological role of an element is linked to its **position in the periodic table**: s-elements act mainly as ions (Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^) in electrolyte and structural roles; p-elements form the skeleton of biomolecules; d-elements, thanks to their variable valence and ability to form complexes, sit in the active center of **metalloenzymes**.

parts.text: One and the same element can be both essential and toxic: it all depends on the **dose**. For example, fluoride strengthens tooth enamel in small doses but causes **fluorosis** in excess; selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy, its excess causes selenosis.

blocks.text: s-Elements are the elements in which the s-orbital of the outer electron shell is being filled: **group IA** (Li, Na, K) — the alkali metals, and **group IIA** (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) — the alkaline earth metals. They are **soft, light, reactive metals**; they give up electrons easily and form stable ions with oxidation states +1 and +2.

**Chemical properties:** they react vigorously with water to form an alkali: 2Na + 2H~2~O → 2NaOH + H~2~↑. Metallic character and reactivity increase down a group (K is more reactive than Na). Their oxides and hydroxides are basic; Ca and Mg salts (carbonates, phosphates) are poorly soluble in water — this is the chemical basis of bone and stone formation.

parts.text: **Hyperkalemia** (K^+^ > 5.5 mmol/L) disturbs cardiac conduction and may lead to asystole; **hypokalemia** causes muscle weakness and arrhythmia. **Hypocalcemia** raises neuromuscular excitability and causes **tetany** (spasms). Lithium salts (Li~2~CO~3~) are used to treat bipolar disorder.

blocks.text: p-Elements are the elements of groups IIIA–VIIIA; p-orbitals are being filled in their outer shell. Non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period: B and Al are amphoteric, C, N, O, S and P are non-metals, and F, Cl, Br and I are the halogens (the most reactive non-metals). Most of them have variable oxidation states (nitrogen from −3 to +5) and form covalent bonds.

parts.text: Uzbekistan is an **iodine-deficiency endemic region**. Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid gland (endemic goiter), and deficiency during pregnancy causes cretinism in the child. This is why table salt is iodized (KIO~3~ is added).

blocks.text: **Dose-dependent effect of fluoride:** about 1 mg/L of fluoride in drinking water prevents caries, because F^−^ replaces OH^−^ in hydroxyapatite Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~(OH)~2~ and forms acid-resistant **fluorapatite** Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~F~2~. More than 1.5 mg/L causes spots on the enamel (fluorosis).

d-Elements (transition metals) are the elements in which the d-orbital of the next-to-outer shell is being filled (groups IB–VIIIB). Their common properties are **variable oxidation states** (Fe^2+^/Fe^3+^, Cu^+^/Cu^2+^), the **formation of complex compounds** and **colored** compounds. These very features make them an essential part of oxidation–reduction enzymes.

sections.title: 9. Nuclear chemistry and its significance in medicine (independent work)

blocks.text: **Radioactivity** is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atomic nuclei, which turn into other nuclei. Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called **isotopes** (for example, ^12^C, ^13^C, ^14^C); radioactive isotopes are called **radionuclides**.

items: **α-decay** — a helium nucleus (^4^He) leaves the nucleus; the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2; it travels only a few micrometers in tissue.
**β^−^-decay** — a neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted; the atomic number rises by 1.
**β^+^-decay** — a proton turns into a neutron and a positron is emitted; the positron annihilates with an electron, giving two γ-quanta (the basis of PET).
**γ-radiation** — a high-energy electromagnetic wave; it has the greatest penetrating power.

blocks.text: **Law of radioactive decay:** N = N~0~·e^−λt^, where λ = ln2 / T~½~. The **half-life** (T~½~) is the time in which half of the radionuclide atoms decay. The unit of activity is the **becquerel** (1 Bq = 1 decay/s); absorbed dose is measured in **grays** (Gy), equivalent dose in **sieverts** (Sv).

skills.title: Skill: identifying cations and anions with qualitative reactions

items: Pour 1–2 mL of the test solution into a clean test tube.
Add the reagent dropwise (3–5 drops) and mix.
Record the observed sign (color of the precipitate, color change, gas).
Check the solubility of the precipitate (for example, add ammonia to AgCl or acetic acid to CaC~2~O~4~).
Write the reaction equation in molecular and ionic form.
Conclusion: state which ion is present in the solution.

skills.title: Skill: identifying a metal ion by its flame color

items: Dip a nichrome (or platinum) wire into concentrated HCl and heat it in the flame until it no longer colors the flame.
Dip the wire into the test salt solution.
Place the wire in the colorless part of the burner flame.
Observe the flame color; for potassium, look through blue cobalt glass (it blocks the yellow color of sodium).
Clean the wire again with HCl after each sample.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient is receiving a 0.9 % sodium chloride solution (normal saline). Take the density of the solution as 1 g/mL (M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol).
cases.ask: How many grams of NaCl are in 500 mL of the solution? What is its molar concentration?
cases.answer: The mass of 500 mL of solution is 500 g; m(NaCl) = 500 · 0.009 = 4.5 g. n(NaCl) = 4.5 / 58.5 = 0.077 mol; C = 0.077 / 0.5 = 0.154 mol/L (≈ 154 mmol/L). Each NaCl gives two ions, so the osmolarity is ≈ 308 mOsm/L — close to blood plasma (isotonic).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A one-year-old child was fed formula prepared with well water. The child’s lips and nails are blue, and the cyanosis does not decrease when oxygen is given. The blood is brownish.
cases.ask: What condition is suspected? What is its chemical basis, and how is it treated?
cases.answer: Nitrate (methemoglobin) poisoning. Nitrates in the well water are reduced to nitrite in the intestine; nitrite oxidizes the Fe^2+^ of hemoglobin to Fe^3+^ — methemoglobin cannot bind O~2~, so giving oxygen does not help. Treatment: methylene blue (it returns Fe^3+^ to Fe^2+^ via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase), ascorbic acid; change the water source.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with thyroid cancer received ^131^I with an activity of 3700 MBq (T~½~ = 8 days).
cases.ask: What activity remains in the body after 24 days (ignore physiological excretion)? Why is ^131^I chosen?
cases.answer: 24 days = 3 half-lives: A = 3700 · (1/2)^3^ = 3700 / 8 = 462.5 MBq. Iodine is actively taken up only by thyroid cells; the β-particles of ^131^I travel a few millimeters in tissue and destroy precisely the gland (tumor) cells, while its γ-radiation allows the process to be followed by scintigraphy.

topics.title: Solutions. Colligative properties of solutions. Fundamentals of titrimetric analysis

goals.text: To teach the student the laws of dissolution of substances and gases in water (Henry’s and Sechenov’s laws), the colligative properties of solutions (Raoult’s and van ’t Hoff’s laws), the ways of expressing concentration, the fundamentals of titrimetric analysis and the neutralization method, and the determination of gastric juice acidity.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: solubility and the factors affecting it, Henry’s and Sechenov’s laws;
Raoult’s law, freezing point depression and boiling point elevation;
the concepts of osmosis, osmotic pressure, van ’t Hoff’s law and the isotonic coefficient;
mass fraction, molar, normal (equivalent) and molal concentration, and titer;
titration, the working solution, the equivalence point, alkalimetry and acidimetry;
the transition ranges of acid–base indicators.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: convert one type of concentration into another;
calculate the osmotic pressure of solutions and distinguish iso-, hypo- and hypertonic solutions;
perform a titration with a burette correctly;
determine and interpret the free, bound and total acidity of gastric juice.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Colligative properties depend **not on the nature of the solute but on the number of particles**. That is why 1 mole of NaCl (2 ions) raises the osmotic pressure about twice as much as 1 mole of glucose.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Indicators: **“Methyl orange — red in acid, Phenolphthalein — pink in alkali”**. Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral media.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The law of equivalents C~n1~·V~1~ = C~n2~·V~2~ is written with **normal** concentration. If molar concentration is used, the stoichiometry of the reaction (for example, H~2~SO~4~ + 2NaOH) must be taken into account separately.

blocks.text: A **solution** is a **homogeneous** system of variable composition made of two or more components. The component present in the larger amount is the **solvent**, and the one in the smaller amount is the **solute**. The main solvent of the body is **water**: it makes up ≈ 60 % of the adult body mass, and thanks to its polarity it dissolves ionic and polar substances well (“like dissolves like”).

**Solubility** is the maximum mass of a substance that can dissolve in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. A solution in this state is called **saturated**. For most solids, solubility increases with temperature; for gases it is the opposite — it **decreases**.
Solubility of gases

**Henry’s law:** at constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid: C = k~H~·p. **Dalton’s law:** from a gas mixture, each gas dissolves according to its own partial pressure.

**Sechenov’s law:** gases are less soluble in electrolyte solutions than in pure water: lg(C~0~ / C) = k·C~salt~. That is why the physical solubility of oxygen in blood plasma is lower than in pure water — most of the oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin.

parts.text: **Caisson (decompression) disease:** at depth, under high pressure, much nitrogen dissolves in the blood. If a diver surfaces quickly, the pressure falls sharply and nitrogen comes out as bubbles that block the vessels (gas embolism). Treatment is to raise the pressure again in a **hyperbaric chamber** and lower it slowly. **Hyperbaric oxygenation** works on the same law.

blocks.text: **Equivalence number (z)**: for an acid — the number of exchangeable H^+^ ions (z = 2 for H~2~SO~4~), for a base — the number of OH^−^ (z = 2 for Ca(OH)~2~), for a salt — the metal valence multiplied by the number of its atoms (z = 6 for Al~2~(SO~4~)~3~). The molar mass of the equivalent is M~eq~ = M / z.
**Conversion formulas:** C = ω·ρ·10 / M (ω in %, ρ in g/mL) and T = C~n~·M~eq~ / 1000. Example: for 36.5 % HCl (ρ = 1.18 g/mL), C = 36.5 · 1.18 · 10 / 36.5 = 11.8 mol/L.

parts.text: In the clinical laboratory, concentrations are given mainly in **mmol/L** (glucose 3.3–5.5 mmol/L), while drug solutions are labeled in **percent** and **mg/mL** (1 % = 10 mg/mL).

blocks.text: Properties of a solution that depend only on the number of particles are called **colligative properties**: lowering of the solvent vapor pressure, freezing point depression, boiling point elevation and osmotic pressure.
**Raoult’s 1st law:** the relative lowering of the solvent vapor pressure above a solution equals the mole fraction of the solute: (p~0~ − p) / p~0~ = χ(solute).

**Raoult’s 2nd law:** the freezing point depression and the boiling point elevation of a solution are proportional to its molal concentration: ΔT~f~ = K·C~m~ (cryometry), ΔT~b~ = E·C~m~ (ebulliometry). For water, the cryoscopic constant K = 1.86 K·kg/mol and the ebullioscopic constant E = 0.52 K·kg/mol.

For electrolytes the **isotonic coefficient** (van ’t Hoff factor) i is introduced into the formulas: i = 1 + α(ν − 1), where α is the degree of dissociation and ν is the number of ions formed from one molecule. For non-electrolytes i = 1.

parts.text: Blood plasma freezes at −0.56 °C. From this its **osmolality** is found: C = 0.56 / 1.86 ≈ 0.3 mol/kg (≈ 300 mOsm/kg). Cryometry (osmometry) is used in the clinic to measure plasma and urine osmolality.

sections.title: 4. Osmosis and osmotic pressure. Van ’t Hoff’s law

blocks.text: **Osmosis** is the one-way diffusion of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from a less concentrated solution into a more concentrated one. The extra pressure that must be applied to the solution to stop osmosis is called the **osmotic pressure** (π).

**Van ’t Hoff’s law:** π = i·C·R·T, where C is the molar concentration (mol/L), R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T is the absolute temperature. The osmotic pressure of blood plasma at 37 °C is **740–780 kPa** (7.3–7.7 atm). About 3.5–4 kPa of it is created by proteins — this is the **oncotic pressure**, which keeps water inside the vessels.

parts.text: Hypertonic solutions are used on purpose in practice: a dressing soaked in **10 % NaCl** draws fluid out of a purulent wound; **25 % MgSO~4~** holds water in the intestine and acts as a laxative; **mannitol** and **15–20 % glucose** draw water from tissue into the blood in cerebral edema. Large intravenous volumes of hypotonic fluid cause hemolysis.

blocks.text: **Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis** is a quantitative method based on measuring the volume of a reagent solution of exactly known concentration that is used up in complete reaction with the analyte. A solution of exactly known concentration is called a **working (standard) solution**; adding it dropwise from a burette to the analyte solution is called **titration**.

The moment when the reagent has reacted with the analyte in an equivalent amount is called the **equivalence point**. It is detected by the color change of an indicator (or by an instrument — a pH meter); the moment actually observed is called the **end point of titration**. The calculation is based on the **law of equivalents**: C~n1~·V~1~ = C~n2~·V~2~.

sections.title: 6. The neutralization method. Alkalimetry and acidimetry

blocks.text: The neutralization method is based on the reaction between acids and bases. **Alkalimetry** is the determination of acids (and acid salts) with a working solution of an alkali (NaOH, KOH); **acidimetry** is the determination of bases (and salts that give an alkaline medium on hydrolysis) with a working solution of an acid (HCl).

The dependence of pH on the volume of titrant added during titration is called the **titration curve**. Near the equivalence point the pH changes sharply — this is the **titration jump**. When 0.1 M HCl is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH, the jump runs from pH 4.3 to 9.7, and pH = 7 at the equivalence point.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Titration curve of a strong acid (0.1 M HCl) with a strong base (0.1 M NaOH) and the color change ranges of indicators (drawn from calculated data).

parts.text: The color change range of the indicator must lie **within the titration jump**. When a weak acid (CH~3~COOH) is titrated with a strong base, the equivalence point lies in the alkaline region (pH ≈ 8.7), so **phenolphthalein** is chosen; when a weak base (NH~3~) is titrated with a strong acid — **methyl orange**.

blocks.text: **Acid–base indicators** are weak organic acids or bases that change color depending on the pH of the medium. According to **Ostwald’s ionic theory**, the undissociated molecule of the indicator (HInd) and its anion (Ind^−^) have different colors: HInd ⇄ H^+^ + Ind^−^. The **chromophore theory** explains the color change by a rearrangement of the molecular structure (chromophore groups).
The color change is seen roughly in the range pH = pK~Ind~ ± 1. The pH value at which the color changes completely is called the **titration index** (pT).

sections.title: 8. Laboratory work: determination of gastric juice acidity

blocks.text: **Principle of the method:** the acids of gastric juice are titrated with a 0.1 M NaOH working solution in the presence of two indicators (Michaelis method). First the **free HCl** is titrated (dimethylaminoazobenzene, pH 2.9–4.0 — the red color turns orange), then, in the same sample, the **total acidity** (phenolphthalein — until a pink color appears). Total acidity includes free HCl, HCl bound to proteins, and acid phosphates and organic acids.
Equipment:
filtered gastric juice, 0.1 M NaOH, 0.5 % alcoholic dimethylaminoazobenzene and 1 % alcoholic phenolphthalein, a burette, a 5 mL pipette, conical flasks.

items: Measure 5 mL of filtered gastric juice into a flask with a pipette.
Add 1 drop of dimethylaminoazobenzene and 2 drops of phenolphthalein (the juice turns red).
Add 0.1 M NaOH dropwise from the burette until the red color turns **orange**; record the volume used (V~1~) — this is the **free HCl**.
Continue the titration: the color first becomes yellow, then a **pink** color appears; titrate until it persists for 30 seconds and record the total volume (V~2~) — this is the **total acidity**.
Calculate the bound acidity: total − free.

blocks.text: Calculation:

Acidity is expressed in **titration units** (t.u.) — the number of milliliters of 0.1 M NaOH needed to neutralize 100 mL of gastric juice. With a 5 mL sample: acidity = V(NaOH) · 20 t.u. Numerically this equals mmol/L.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient’s gastric juice was examined. When 5 mL of filtered juice was titrated, 0.4 mL of 0.1 M NaOH was used to the dimethylaminoazobenzene end point and a total of 1.2 mL to the phenolphthalein end point.
cases.ask: Calculate and interpret the free, bound and total acidity.
cases.answer: Free HCl = 0.4 · 20 = 8 t.u.; total acidity = 1.2 · 20 = 24 t.u.; bound = 24 − 8 = 16 t.u. Total acidity (normal 40–60) and free HCl (normal 20–40) are reduced — **hypoacidity**. This is typical of chronic atrophic gastritis; the patient should be referred for gastroscopy and biopsy.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A hypertonic solution is needed to clean a purulent wound. The laboratory assistant prepared a 10 % NaCl solution (ρ = 1.07 g/mL, M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol, i = 1.9).
cases.ask: Calculate the osmotic pressure of the solution at 37 °C. Why does it act on the wound?
cases.answer: C = 10 · 1.07 · 10 / 58.5 = 1.83 mol/L. π = i·C·R·T = 1.9 · 1.83 · 8.314 · 310 ≈ 8960 kPa — about 12 times higher than the plasma pressure (740–780 kPa). By osmosis, water is drawn from the wound tissue and pus into the dressing, and the wound is cleaned.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: In an emergency, a patient was mistakenly given 1 liter of distilled water intravenously. Soon the urine turned reddish and pain appeared in the lower back.
cases.ask: What happened? Explain the physicochemical basis.
cases.answer: Distilled water is hypotonic to plasma. By osmosis, water enters the red blood cells, makes them swell and burst — **hemolysis**. Free hemoglobin passes into the urine (hemoglobinuria) and may block the renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury. Only isotonic solutions (0.9 % NaCl, 5 % glucose) or other solutions prescribed for a medical indication are given intravenously.

goals.text: To teach the student Werner’s coordination theory, the structure, naming and stability in solution of complex compounds, the nature of their chemical bonds, inner complex compounds (chelates) and chelation therapy, the fundamentals of complexometry and the determination of calcium in blood serum; to explain the chemical basis of stone diseases.
By the end of the class the student should know:

the classification and naming rules of complex compounds;
instability and stability constants;
the donor–acceptor bond and hybridization in complex compounds;
chelates, the chelate effect and biologically important complexes (heme, chlorophyll, B~12~);

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Trilon B (EDTA) reacts with metal ions in a **1 : 1** ratio whatever their charge. This makes the calculation in complexometry very simple: n(Me) = n(Trilon B).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Order for reading a complex formula: **“Ligand — number — center — charge”**: [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^ is the tetra**ammine**copper(II) ion.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In lead poisoning, **calcium disodium** edetate (CaNa~2~EDTA) is used. Calcium-free Na~2~EDTA also binds the Ca^2+^ of the blood and causes life-threatening hypocalcemia.

blocks.text: **Complex compounds** are compounds that contain molecules or ions (ligands) arranged in a definite order around a central atom (ion) and that exist as separate particles even in solution. Their structure was explained in 1893 by **A. Werner** (Nobel Prize in 1913).

items: **Complexing agent (central atom)** — usually an ion of a d-element: Fe^2+^, Fe^3+^, Cu^2+^, Co^3+^, Zn^2+^, Ag^+^, Pt^2+^.
**Ligands** — molecules or anions bound to the central atom: H~2~O, NH~3~, Cl^−^, CN^−^, OH^−^, amino acids.
**Coordination number** — the number of donor atoms bound directly to the central atom (most often 2, 4 or 6).
**Inner sphere** — the central atom and the ligands, written in square brackets; **outer sphere** — the ions outside the brackets, which separate easily in solution.

blocks.text: For example, in K~4~[Fe(CN)~6~]: the central ion is Fe^2+^, the ligand is CN^−^, the coordination number is 6, the inner sphere is [Fe(CN)~6~]^4−^ and the outer sphere is 4K^+^. The charge of the complex ion = charge of the central ion + charges of the ligands: (+2) + 6·(−1) = −4.

The number of bonds a ligand forms with the central atom is called its **denticity**: **monodentate** (NH~3~, H~2~O, Cl^−^, CN^−^), **bidentate** (ethylenediamine, oxalate, glycinate), **polydentate** (EDTA — 6-dentate, hexadentate).

parts.text: **Cisplatin** [Pt(NH~3~)~2~Cl~2~] is the best-known complex drug. In the cell its chloride ligands are replaced by water, and platinum binds to the nitrogen of guanine in DNA, “stitching” the strands together — division of the tumor cell stops. It is used in testicular, ovarian and lung cancer; its main adverse effect is nephrotoxicity.

sections.title: 2. Equilibrium and stability of complex compounds in solution

blocks.text: In solution a complex compound first dissociates completely along the outer sphere (like a strong electrolyte): [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]Cl → [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ + Cl^−^. The inner sphere breaks down only very slightly and stepwise: [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ ⇄ Ag^+^ + 2NH~3~.

This equilibrium is described by the **instability constant**: K~inst~ = [Ag^+^]·[NH~3~]^2^ / [[Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^]. Its reciprocal is the **stability constant**: β = 1 / K~inst~. The smaller K~inst~, the more stable the complex.

blocks.text: Formation of a stable complex can dissolve poorly soluble substances: AgCl dissolves in ammonia because the Ag^+^ ions are bound into [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^, and [Ag^+^] in solution falls below the solubility product of AgCl. Conversely, a strong precipitating agent destroys a complex: when KI is added to [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^, AgI precipitates.

sections.title: 3. The nature of the chemical bond in complex compounds

blocks.text: The bond between the central atom and a ligand is a **donor–acceptor (coordinate)** bond: the ligand (donor) supplies a lone electron pair and the central atom (acceptor) takes it into its empty orbitals. According to valence bond theory, the orbitals of the central atom hybridize, and the geometry of the complex depends on the type of hybridization.

blocks.text: **Crystal field theory** shows that the electric field of the ligands splits the d-orbitals of the central atom by energy. Visible light is absorbed when an electron moves from one d-level to another — that is why complexes of d-elements are **colored**: [Cu(H~2~O)~4~]^2+^ is light blue, [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^ deep blue, hemoglobin red.

Compounds in which a polydentate ligand forms several bonds with the central atom and so creates a **ring (cycle)** are called **inner complex compounds** or **chelates** (Greek *chele* — a crab’s claw). The most stable are chelates with **five- and six-membered** rings.

blocks.text: **The chelate effect:** even with the same donor atoms, a chelate is much more stable than a complex with monodentate ligands. The reason is entropy: one polydentate ligand displaces several water molecules, and the number of particles in solution increases (ΔS > 0).

blocks.text: **Chelation therapy** is the removal of toxic metal ions from the body by binding them into stable, water-soluble chelates that are excreted by the kidneys. The drug (complexing agent) must form a **more stable** complex with the toxic metal than with the essential metals of the body (Ca, Zn).

parts.text: **Pearson’s HSAB principle** (“soft with soft, hard with hard”): soft metals (Hg^2+^, Pb^2+^, Cd^2+^, As^3+^) bind stably to **sulfur** ligands, hard ions (Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^, Fe^3+^) to **oxygen** ligands. That is why thiol antidotes are used against mercury and arsenic.

blocks.text: **Complexometry** is a method based on titrating metal ions with a complexone (most often **Trilon B**, the disodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, Na~2~H~2~Y·2H~2~O). Trilon B forms a stable chelate with metal ions in a 1 : 1 ratio whatever their charge: Me^2+^ + H~2~Y^2−^ → MeY^2−^ + 2H^+^.

items: Because H^+^ is released in the reaction, the titration is done in the presence of a **buffer**: an ammonia buffer (pH ≈ 10) for the sum of Ca^2+^ + Mg^2+^, and NaOH (pH 12–13, Mg(OH)~2~ precipitates) for Ca^2+^ alone.

**Metal indicators** form colored complexes with the metal that are less stable than those with Trilon B: **eriochrome black T** (pH 10: wine-red with the metal, blue when free), **murexide** (pH 12: pink with Ca, violet when free).
At the equivalence point Trilon B pulls the metal out of the indicator complex, and the color of the free indicator appears.

parts.text: Complexometry is used to determine water **hardness** (the sum of Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^, meq/L). Hard water increases the tendency to form kidney stones and gallstones; in some regions of Uzbekistan (Khorezm, Karakalpakstan) the hardness of drinking water is above the standard (7 meq/L).

blocks.text: Formation and study of complex compounds

items: **Copper ammine complex:** add NH~3~·H~2~O dropwise to CuSO~4~ solution — first a light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)~2~ forms, then it dissolves in excess ammonia to give deep blue [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^.

**Silver ammine complex:** add NaCl to AgNO~3~ (white AgCl), then add ammonia — the precipitate dissolves; add KI to the resulting solution — a yellow precipitate of AgI forms (the complex is destroyed).
**Prussian blue:** add K~4~[Fe(CN)~6~] to FeCl~3~ — a deep blue precipitate.
**Detecting the central ion in a complex ion:** add NaOH to K~3~[Fe(CN)~6~] solution — no Fe(OH)~3~ precipitate forms, because Fe^3+^ is held inside a stable complex.
Write an equation for each experiment and explain the observation.

blocks.text: Complexometric determination of calcium in blood serum

**Principle of the method:** in an alkaline medium (pH 12–13) the Ca^2+^ of serum forms a pink complex with murexide; on titration with Trilon B the calcium passes into the more stable CaY^2−^, and the color turns **violet**.

items: Place 1 mL of blood serum and 1 mL of distilled water in a flask.
Add 0.2 mL of 1 M NaOH and a pinch of a dry murexide mixture (with NaCl, 1 : 100) — the solution turns pink.
Titrate from a microburette with 0.0025 M Trilon B solution until the color turns violet.
Titrate a blank (without serum) in the same way and subtract the volume used.
Calculate: C(Ca^2+^) = C(Trilon B) · V(Trilon B) / V(serum).

blocks.text: **Example:** 0.96 mL of Trilon B was used in the titration. C(Ca) = 0.0025 · 0.96 / 1 = 0.0024 mol/L = **2.4 mmol/L** — normal (total calcium 2.2–2.6 mmol/L).

parts.text: **Hypercalcemia** (> 2.6 mmol/L) occurs in hyperparathyroidism, tumor metastases and hypervitaminosis D; **hypocalcemia** (< 2.2 mmol/L) in hypoparathyroidism, rickets, renal failure and acute pancreatitis. About 40 % of total calcium is bound to albumin, so the result is corrected in hypoalbuminemia.

sections.title: 8. Chemical basis of stone diseases (independent work)

blocks.text: Stones (calculi) form in a biological fluid when the concentration of the ions of a poorly soluble salt exceeds its **solubility product** (K~sp~), that is, when the fluid is **supersaturated**: [Ca^2+^]·[C~2~O~4~^2−^] > K~sp~(CaC~2~O~4~) = 2.3·10^−9^. Once a crystal nucleus forms, new layers are deposited on it.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A battery factory worker complains of colicky abdominal pain, weakness and headache. There is a gray line on his gums; the blood shows hypochromic anemia and basophilic stippling of red cells.
cases.ask: What poisoning is suspected? Which complexing agent is used to treat it, and why is its calcium form chosen?
cases.answer: Chronic lead poisoning (saturnism). Pb^2+^ blocks the enzymes of heme synthesis (δ-ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) — anemia develops. Treatment: edetate calcium disodium (CaNa~2~EDTA) intravenously; Pb^2+^ forms a more stable complex with EDTA than Ca^2+^ does, displaces the calcium, and PbY^2−^ is excreted in the urine. Calcium-free Na~2~EDTA would bind the blood calcium and could cause hypocalcemia and cardiac arrest. In children, succimer (DMSA) is given by mouth.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: To determine a patient’s serum calcium, 1 mL of serum was titrated with 0.0025 M Trilon B. Three titrations used 0.70, 0.72 and 0.71 mL, and the blank used 0.01 mL.
cases.ask: Calculate and interpret the calcium concentration. In which diseases can such a result occur?
cases.answer: Mean volume = 0.71 mL; subtracting the blank gives 0.70 mL. C(Ca) = 0.0025 · 0.70 / 1 = 0.00175 mol/L = 1.75 mmol/L — **hypocalcemia** (normal 2.2–2.6). Causes: hypoparathyroidism (for example, after thyroid surgery), vitamin D deficiency, chronic renal failure, acute pancreatitis. The albumin level should also be checked.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old man has gout and renal colic. Urine pH is 5.0; no stones are seen on X-ray, but ultrasound shows a stone in the kidney.
cases.ask: What type of stone is it? What is the chemically based treatment?
cases.answer: A uric acid (urate) stone: in acidic urine (pH < 5.5) uric acid is poorly soluble and crystallizes; urate stones are not visible on X-ray. Treatment is to alkalinize the urine with **potassium citrate** to pH 6.5–7.0: uric acid passes into the soluble urate ion (anionic form) and the stone may dissolve; plenty of fluids, allopurinol (reduces uric acid formation), and limiting purine-rich food.

sections.title: 1. The ion product of water and the hydrogen ion exponent

blocks.text: Water is a very weak electrolyte: H~2~O ⇄ H^+^ + OH^−^. At 25 °C the **ion product of water** K~w~ = [H^+^]·[OH^−^] = 10^−14^. In a neutral medium [H^+^] = [OH^−^] = 10^−7^ mol/L.
The **hydrogen ion exponent** pH = −lg[H^+^], the **hydroxide exponent** pOH = −lg[OH^−^], and pH + pOH = 14. pH < 7 is acidic, pH = 7 neutral and pH > 7 alkaline.

items: **Strong acid:** pH = −lg C (for 0.01 M HCl, pH = 2).
**Strong base:** pOH = −lg C, pH = 14 − pOH (for 0.01 M NaOH, pH = 12).
**Weak acid:** pH = ½(pK~a~ − lg C) (for 0.1 M CH~3~COOH, pK~a~ = 4.76, pH = 2.88).

sections.title: 2. The concept of buffer systems and their classification

blocks.text: A **buffer system** is a solution that keeps its pH almost constant when small amounts of a strong acid or alkali are added, and also on dilution. It consists of two components: a proton donor (a weak acid) and a proton acceptor (its salt — the conjugate base).

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Classification of buffer systems

Composition

rows: a weak acid + its salt with a strong base
a weak base + its salt with a strong acid

blocks.text: Take the acetate buffer as an example: the solution contains large amounts of CH~3~COOH (poorly dissociated) and CH~3~COO^−^ (formed completely from the salt).

items: **When an acid is added**, the H^+^ ions are bound by the anion of the salt: CH~3~COO^−^ + H^+^ → CH~3~COOH. A strong acid is replaced by a weak one, and the pH falls only slightly.
**When an alkali is added**, the OH^−^ ions are neutralized by the weak acid: CH~3~COOH + OH^−^ → CH~3~COO^−^ + H~2~O. The pH rises only slightly.
**On dilution** the ratio of the components does not change, so the pH hardly changes either.

parts.text: The same happens in blood: HCO~3~^−^ + H^+^ → H~2~CO~3~ → CO~2~↑ + H~2~O (CO~2~ is exhaled by the lungs); H~2~CO~3~ + OH^−^ → HCO~3~^−^ + H~2~O. The strength of the bicarbonate buffer is that it is an **open system**: the lungs regulate CO~2~ and the kidneys HCO~3~^−^.

sections.title: 4. Calculating the pH of buffer solutions. Buffer capacity

blocks.text: **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation:** for an acidic buffer pH = pK~a~ + lg([salt] / [acid]); for a basic buffer pOH = pK~b~ + lg([salt] / [base]), pH = 14 − pOH. When the component concentrations are equal, pH = pK~a~.

**Example:** in a 1 : 1 mixture of 0.1 M CH~3~COOH and 0.1 M CH~3~COONa, pH = 4.76 + lg1 = 4.76. If 0.01 mol of HCl is added to 1 L of this buffer: [salt] = 0.09, [acid] = 0.11; pH = 4.76 + lg(0.09 / 0.11) = 4.67 — the pH changed by only 0.09. If the same amount of HCl is added to 1 L of water, the pH falls from 7 to 2.

**Buffer capacity** (B) is the number of moles of equivalent of a strong acid or alkali that must be added to 1 L of buffer solution to change its pH by 1 unit: B = Δn / (ΔpH · V). Buffer capacity is greater the higher the **concentration** of the components and the closer their **ratio is to 1 : 1**.

blocks.text: The **bicarbonate buffer** is the main buffer of the extracellular fluid. In plasma [HCO~3~^−^] = 22–26 mmol/L and [H~2~CO~3~] = 0.03 · pCO~2~ = 0.03 · 40 = 1.2 mmol/L; the ratio is 24 : 1.2 = 20 : 1.

The **phosphate buffer** is the main buffer of the intracellular fluid and of urine; in blood [HPO~4~^2−^] : [H~2~PO~4~^−^] = 4 : 1 (pH = 6.8 + lg4 = 7.4). In the renal tubules it excretes H^+^ ions into the urine as H~2~PO~4~^−^ (titratable acidity).

The **hemoglobin buffer** works in the tissues and the lungs: oxyhemoglobin is a stronger acid than deoxyhemoglobin. After giving up O~2~ in the tissues, Hb becomes a weaker acid and binds H^+^ (formed from CO~2~); in the lungs the reverse happens (the Bohr effect).

parts.text: The **alkaline reserve of the blood** is the amount of CO~2~ that 100 mL of plasma can bind at pCO~2~ = 40 mmHg: normally **50–70 vol %**. In modern practice it has been replaced by **standard bicarbonate** (SB, 22–26 mmol/L) and **base excess** (BE, 0 ± 2.3 mmol/L).

blocks.text: Blood pH **below 7.35** is **acidosis**, **above 7.45** is **alkalosis**. By origin, **respiratory** (related to breathing; the primary change is in pCO~2~) and **metabolic** (the primary change is in HCO~3~^−^) types are distinguished. The body **compensates** a disorder through the other system: a metabolic one through breathing, a respiratory one through the kidneys.

sections.title: 8. Urine pH and stone formation (independent work)

blocks.text: The kidneys excrete excess acid (≈ 50–100 mmol of H^+^ per day) as phosphate buffer (titratable acidity) and ammonium (NH~4~^+^). That is why urine pH varies from 4.5 to 8.0 depending on diet and disease, and it directly affects stone formation.

items: **Acidic urine** (meat diet, gout, metabolic syndrome) — uric acid is poorly dissociated and crystallizes: **urate stones**.
**Alkaline urine** (plant diet, infection with urease-producing bacteria — Proteus) — phosphate salts precipitate: **phosphate and struvite stones**.
In treatment, urine pH is changed on purpose: it is alkalinized with potassium citrate for urates and acidified for phosphates.

items: Look at the pH: < 7.35 — acidosis, > 7.45 — alkalosis.

Assess HCO~3~^−^ (normal 22–26 mmol/L): if it changed in the same direction as pH — a metabolic disorder.
A change in the second parameter shows compensation.
Compare with the clinical situation to find the cause.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus was brought in unconscious. His breathing is deep and noisy, and there is a smell of acetone from the mouth. Blood gases: pH 7.12; pCO~2~ = 22 mmHg; HCO~3~^−^ = 8 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Identify the acid–base disorder. How is compensation taking place?
cases.answer: Metabolic acidosis (pH ↓, HCO~3~^−^ ↓ — in the same direction): diabetic ketoacidosis. Ketone bodies (acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids) use up the bicarbonate buffer. Compensation is respiratory: deep noisy **Kussmaul breathing** removes CO~2~ and has lowered pCO~2~ to 22, but the pH has not returned to normal (partial compensation). Treatment: insulin, fluids, potassium monitoring.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A laboratory assistant needs 20 mL of phosphate buffer with pH 7.4. She has 1/15 M Na~2~HPO~4~ and 1/15 M KH~2~PO~4~ solutions (pK~a~ = 6.8).
cases.ask: How much of each solution should be taken?
cases.answer: pH = pK~a~ + lg([salt] / [acid]); 7.4 = 6.8 + lg x; lg x = 0.6; x = 4. So salt : acid = 4 : 1. For 20 mL: Na~2~HPO~4~ — 16 mL, KH~2~PO~4~ — 4 mL. The pH should be checked with a pH meter.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with pyloric stenosis has been vomiting heavily for a week. Blood gases: pH 7.52; pCO~2~ = 48 mmHg; HCO~3~^−^ = 36 mmol/L; K^+^ = 3.0 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Identify the type of disorder and explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: Metabolic alkalosis (pH ↑, HCO~3~^−^ ↑). Vomiting removes gastric HCl; while producing HCl, the gastric cells release HCO~3~^−^ into the blood, which is now not neutralized. Hypovolemia and hypokalemia enhance HCO~3~^−^ reabsorption in the kidney and maintain the alkalosis. Compensation is hypoventilation (pCO~2~ has risen to 48). Treatment: 0.9 % NaCl and KCl solutions, correction of the stenosis.

topics.title: Chemical thermodynamics. Determining the heat effect of chemical reactions

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of thermodynamic systems and state functions, types of energy, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy, Hess’s law and its corollaries, and specific heat capacity; to teach the calorimetric determination of the heat effect of a reaction and the application of this knowledge to energy metabolism in the body.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: open, closed and isolated systems and state functions;
the concepts of heat, work, internal energy and specific heat capacity;
the 1st law of thermodynamics and enthalpy;
the 2nd law of thermodynamics, entropy and Gibbs free energy;
Hess’s law and its corollaries;
the thermodynamic basis of energy production and expenditure in the body.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the heat effect of a reaction from enthalpies of formation;
decide from the sign of ΔG whether a process can occur spontaneously;
measure and calculate the heat of neutralization in a calorimeter;
calculate the energy value of nutrients.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A process occurs spontaneously if **ΔG < 0** (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS). In an exothermic reaction ΔH < 0 (heat is released), in an endothermic one ΔH > 0 (heat is absorbed).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Energy value: **“4 — 4 — 9”** kcal/g: carbohydrates — 4, proteins — 4, fats — 9 (alcohol — 7).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Thermodynamics answers whether a reaction **can occur**, but not **how fast** it goes. The oxidation of glucose has ΔG < 0, yet glucose does not burn spontaneously in air — an enzyme (catalyst) is needed.

blocks.text: **Chemical thermodynamics** is the science that studies the conversion of energy from one form to another in chemical and physical processes, and the direction of processes and the conditions of equilibrium. Its laws apply fully to the living organism as well — this is studied by **bioenergetics**.

blocks.text: **State functions** are quantities whose value depends only on the initial and final state of the system, not on the path between them: internal energy (U), enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and Gibbs energy (G). Heat (Q) and work (A), on the other hand, are not state functions.

**Specific heat capacity** (c) is the amount of heat needed to warm 1 g of a substance by 1 K, J/(g·K). Amount of heat: Q = c·m·ΔT. Water has a very high specific heat capacity — **4.18 J/(g·K)**; that is why water (≈ 60 % of body mass) keeps body temperature stable. Energy units: 1 cal = 4.184 J.

parts.text: **Types of energy:** kinetic and potential, thermal, chemical (bond energy), electrical, light and mechanical. In the body, the chemical energy of nutrients is converted into the energy of ATP, and then into mechanical (muscle), electrical (nerve impulse), osmotic (ion transport) and chemical (synthesis) work; the rest is released as heat.

blocks.text: **The 1st law of thermodynamics** (the law of conservation of energy): heat supplied to a system is used to increase its internal energy and to do work against external forces: Q = ΔU + A, where A = p·ΔV. Energy is neither created nor destroyed; it only changes from one form to another.

Most chemical and biological processes occur at **constant pressure**. In this case the heat effect equals the change in **enthalpy**: Q~p~ = ΔH, where H = U + pV. Values measured at standard conditions (298 K, 101.3 kPa) are marked with °: ΔH°.

items: **Exothermic** reaction — heat is released, ΔH < 0 (combustion, neutralization, oxidation of glucose).
**Endothermic** reaction — heat is absorbed, ΔH > 0 (decomposition of CaCO~3~, dissolution of NH~4~NO~3~ in water).
**Thermochemical equation** — an equation showing the heat effect and the physical states of the substances: H~2~(g) + ½O~2~(g) → H~2~O(l); ΔH° = −285.8 kJ.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Energy diagram of exothermic (ΔH < 0) and endothermic (ΔH > 0) reactions; E~a~ is the activation energy (diagram).

blocks.text: **Hess’s law** (1840): the heat effect of a reaction depends only on the nature and state of the initial and final substances, and not on the path (number of steps) by which the reaction takes place. For example, whether glucose is oxidized in the body in dozens of steps or burns instantly in a calorimeter, the total heat released is the same.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Hess’s law: the heat of direct combustion of carbon to CO~2~ equals the heat of two-step combustion through CO: ΔH~1~ = ΔH~2~ + ΔH~3~ (diagram).

items: **1st corollary:** the heat effect of a reaction equals the sum of the enthalpies of formation of the products minus the sum of the enthalpies of formation of the reactants: ΔH°~r~ = ΣΔH°~f~(products) − ΣΔH°~f~(reactants). The enthalpy of formation of simple substances (O~2~, H~2~, C graphite) is 0.

**2nd corollary:** the heat effect equals the sum of the enthalpies of combustion of the reactants minus the sum of the enthalpies of combustion of the products: ΔH°~r~ = ΣΔH°~c~(reactants) − ΣΔH°~c~(products).
**Lavoisier–Laplace law:** the heat effects of the forward and reverse reactions are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.

sections.title: 4. The 2nd law of thermodynamics. Entropy and Gibbs energy

blocks.text: **Entropy** (S) is a measure of the disorder of a system; the Boltzmann equation is S = k·lnW (W is the number of possible microstates of the system). Entropy **increases** in the transitions solid → liquid → gas, on dissolution, and when molecules break down and the number of particles grows.
**The 2nd law of thermodynamics:** in an isolated system, spontaneous processes proceed with an increase in entropy (ΔS > 0). Heat flows spontaneously only from a hot body to a cold one.

In closed and open systems the criterion of direction is the **Gibbs free energy**: ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS. ΔG < 0 — the process occurs spontaneously (**exergonic**), ΔG > 0 — it does not occur spontaneously (**endergonic**), ΔG = 0 — equilibrium. The standard Gibbs energy is related to the equilibrium constant: ΔG° = −R·T·lnK.

parts.text: A living organism is an **open system**: it maintains a high internal order (low entropy) by taking ordered nutrients from the environment and releasing disordered products (CO~2~, H~2~O, heat) (I. Prigogine). Death is the stopping of the order-maintaining mechanisms and an increase in entropy.

blocks.text: Many necessary reactions in the body are endergonic (ΔG > 0). They take place through **energy coupling** (coupled reactions): an endergonic reaction is linked by one enzyme with an exergonic reaction — most often **ATP hydrolysis**; if the total ΔG is negative, both proceed.

items: ATP + H~2~O → ADP + H~3~PO~4~; ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol.
Glucose + H~3~PO~4~ → glucose 6-phosphate + H~2~O; ΔG°′ = +13.8 kJ/mol.
Coupled reaction: glucose + ATP → glucose 6-phosphate + ADP; ΔG°′ = −30.5 + 13.8 = −16.7 kJ/mol (hexokinase).

parts.text: ATP is the **energy “currency”**: it does not store energy but carries it from where it is produced (the mitochondria) to where it is used. A person resynthesizes and breaks down an amount of ATP close to his own body mass every day.

sections.title: 6. Laboratory work: determining the heat effect of a neutralization reaction

blocks.text: **Principle of the method:** when a strong acid is neutralized by a strong base, only the reaction H^+^ + OH^−^ → H~2~O occurs, so the heat effect does not depend on the nature of the acid and base: ΔH° ≈ −57 kJ/mol. The heat released is calculated from the rise in temperature of the solution in the calorimeter.
Equipment:
a simple calorimeter (two beakers: an inner beaker and an insulating layer, a lid), a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C, measuring cylinders, 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH solutions.

items: Pour 50 mL of 1 M HCl into the inner beaker of the calorimeter and record its temperature (t~1~) after 3–5 minutes.
Measure the temperature of 50 mL of 1 M NaOH in another cylinder (it should equal t~1~).
Quickly pour the NaOH into the calorimeter, close the lid and stir with the thermometer.
Record the highest temperature reached (t~2~).
Calculate the heat effect.

blocks.text: Calculation:

Mass of solution m = 100 g (ρ ≈ 1 g/mL), c = 4.18 J/(g·K). For example, if ΔT = t~2~ − t~1~ = 6.7 K: Q = 4.18 · 100 · 6.7 = 2800 J. Amount of substance reacted n = 1 · 0.05 = 0.05 mol. ΔH = −Q / n = −2800 / 0.05 = −56 000 J/mol = **−56 kJ/mol**. The difference from the theoretical value (≈ 2 %) is due to heat absorbed by the calorimeter walls and heat losses.

parts.text: Heats of dissolution are also used in medicine: in **cold packs** NH~4~NO~3~ absorbs heat when it dissolves in water (ΔH > 0) — they are used for injuries and fever; **hot packs** use exothermic processes such as the dissolution of CaCl~2~ or the oxidation of iron.

sections.title: 7. Energy production and expenditure in metabolism (independent work)

blocks.text: The body obtains energy from the oxidation of nutrients. The common pathway of catabolism is acetyl-CoA, the Krebs cycle and the respiratory chain; ≈ 40 % of the energy is converted into ATP, and the rest is released as **heat**, which maintains body temperature.

items: **Basal metabolism** is the minimum energy expenditure needed for life at rest, fasting, at a comfortable temperature: in adults ≈ 1600–1800 kcal (≈ 7000 kJ) per day.
**Total daily expenditure** depends on physical activity: mental work — 2500–2800 kcal, heavy physical work — 3500–4500 kcal.
**Direct calorimetry** measures the heat released by the body in a special chamber; **indirect calorimetry** calculates it from O~2~ consumption and CO~2~ release.
**Respiratory quotient** (RQ = V(CO~2~) / V(O~2~)): carbohydrates — 1.0, proteins — 0.8, fats — 0.7; on a mixed diet ≈ 0.85.

parts.text: Energy balance: if intake exceeds expenditure, the excess energy is stored as **fat** (1 kg of adipose tissue ≈ 7700 kcal). Thyroid hormones raise basal metabolism (weight loss in thyrotoxicosis, weight gain in hypothyroidism).

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient eats 300 g of carbohydrates, 80 g of protein and 70 g of fat per day.
cases.ask: Calculate the energy value of the diet in kcal and kJ. Does it cover the expenditure of a person doing mental work?
cases.answer: Carbohydrates: 300 · 4.1 = 1230 kcal; proteins: 80 · 4.1 = 328 kcal; fats: 70 · 9.3 = 651 kcal. Total ≈ 2209 kcal ≈ 9242 kJ (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ). The expenditure of a person doing mental work is 2500–2800 kcal — the diet falls slightly short, and in the long term body mass will decrease.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: In the body, glucose is oxidized to CO~2~ and H~2~O in dozens of steps through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the respiratory chain. In a calorimeter it burns in an instant.
cases.ask: In which case is more heat released? Justify your answer and calculate ΔH for 1 mole of glucose (ΔH°~f~: glucose −1273.3; CO~2~ −393.5; H~2~O −285.8 kJ/mol).
cases.answer: According to Hess’s law the total heat effect is the same in both cases, because the initial and final substances are the same: ΔH = 6·(−393.5) + 6·(−285.8) − (−1273.3) = −2802.5 kJ/mol. The difference is that in the body part of this energy (≈ 40 %) goes not into heat but into ATP, and is then used to do work.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: In a calorimeter, 50 mL of 1 M HCl and 50 mL of 1 M NaOH were mixed; the temperature rose from 21.0 °C to 27.6 °C (c = 4.18 J/(g·K), ρ = 1 g/mL).
cases.ask: Calculate the heat of neutralization and compare it with the theoretical value.
cases.answer: ΔT = 6.6 K; Q = 4.18 · 100 · 6.6 = 2759 J; n = 0.05 mol; ΔH = −2759 / 0.05 = −55 180 J/mol ≈ −55.2 kJ/mol. The theoretical value is ≈ −57 kJ/mol, and the relative error is ≈ 3 %: the calorimeter walls and the thermometer absorbed part of the heat, and part was lost to the air.

topics.title: Fundamentals of electrochemistry. Electrical conductivity. Conductometry. Electrode processes. Formation and types of potentials. Potentiometry

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the electrical conductivity of electrolyte solutions, conductometry and conductometric titration, the formation of electrode, redox, membrane and diffusion potentials, galvanic cells, electrodes and the fundamentals of potentiometry, and the use of electrochemical methods in medicine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: conductors of the first and second kind, specific and molar conductivity;
Kohlrausch’s law and Ostwald’s dilution law;
conductometric titration curves;
the Nernst equation, the standard hydrogen electrode and standard potentials;
redox, membrane and diffusion potentials;
galvanic cells, reference and indicator electrodes, and potentiometry.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate electrode and membrane potentials with the Nernst equation;
calculate the EMF of a galvanic cell and write its scheme;
determine the direction of a redox reaction from the potentials;
interpret the results of electrochemical medical tests.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Nernst equation (25 °C): E = E° + (0.059 / n)·lg[Me^n+^]. When the concentration of a singly charged ion changes **10-fold**, the potential changes by **59 mV** (by 61 mV at 37 °C).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“An Ox, Red Cat”**: **An**ode — **Ox**idation, **Red**uction — **Cat**hode. In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative pole.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A redox reaction proceeds spontaneously between the oxidant of the pair with the **higher potential** and the reductant of the pair with the **lower potential**: if ΔE > 0, then ΔG = −nFΔE < 0.

blocks.text: Substances that conduct electric current are of two kinds: **conductors of the first kind** (metals, graphite), in which the current is carried by electrons, and **conductors of the second kind** (electrolyte solutions and melts), in which it is carried by ions. Body tissues are conductors of the second kind.

items: **Specific conductivity** (κ) is the conductance of a column of solution 1 m^2^ in cross-section and 1 m long, S/m (siemens per meter).
**Molar conductivity** (λ) is the conductance of a solution containing 1 mole of electrolyte: λ = κ / C, S·m^2^/mol. On dilution λ increases and reaches its maximum value (λ~∞~) at infinite dilution.
**Kohlrausch’s law:** at infinite dilution the molar conductivity equals the sum of the cation and anion mobilities: λ~∞~ = λ~+~ + λ~−~.
The **degree of dissociation** of a weak electrolyte: α = λ / λ~∞~. **Ostwald’s dilution law**: K = α^2^·C / (1 − α); if α ≪ 1, α ≈ √(K / C).

blocks.text: H^+^ and OH^−^ ions are several times more mobile than other ions: they move by proton “hopping” along chains of water molecules (the relay mechanism). That is why solutions of acids and alkalis conduct current better than salt solutions.

parts.text: The electrical conductivity of tissues depends on their water and electrolyte content: blood, lymph, cerebrospinal fluid and muscle conduct well, while adipose tissue, bone and dry skin conduct poorly. This is the basis of **bioimpedance analysis** (body composition — the share of fat and water), **rheography** (the blood filling of an organ) and **electrophoresis** (delivery of drug ions through the skin).

blocks.text: **Conductometry** is an analytical method based on measuring the electrical conductivity of a solution. **Direct conductometry** determines the purity of water, the salt content of a solution and the dissociation constant of a weak electrolyte. In **conductometric titration** the equivalence point is found from the break point of the conductivity graph; it is convenient for colored and turbid solutions (where an indicator does not work).

When HCl is titrated with NaOH, the mobile H^+^ ions are replaced by the less mobile Na^+^ ions and the conductivity **decreases**; it is minimal at the equivalence point; then it **increases** again because of the excess mobile OH^−^ ions.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Conductometric titration curves: titration of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak acid (CH~3~COOH) with NaOH; the equivalence point is where the lines intersect (calculated from ion mobilities).

blocks.text: When a metal is placed in a solution of its salt, an **electrical double layer** forms at the metal–solution boundary: reactive metals (Zn) pass into the solution as ions and leave a negative charge behind, while less reactive metals (Cu) take up their ions from the solution and become positively charged. The potential difference arising at this boundary is called the **electrode potential**.

The absolute value of an electrode potential cannot be measured, so it is measured relative to the **standard hydrogen electrode** (E° = 0, p(H~2~) = 101.3 kPa, a(H^+^) = 1 mol/L). The value measured under standard conditions is called the **standard electrode potential** (E°); when metals are arranged in order of increasing E°, the **electrochemical series** is obtained.
**Nernst equation:** E = E° + (R·T / n·F)·ln[Me^n+^], or at 25 °C E = E° + (0.059 / n)·lg[Me^n+^], where n is the number of electrons and F = 96 485 C/mol (the Faraday constant).

blocks.text: A **redox potential** arises when an inert electrode (platinum) is placed in a solution containing the oxidized and reduced forms of a substance. **Nernst–Peters equation:** E = E° + (0.059 / n)·lg([Ox] / [Red]). For example, for the Fe^3+^/Fe^2+^ pair E° = +0.77 V.

In biochemistry, standard potentials at pH = 7 (E°′) are used. The Gibbs energy of a redox reaction: ΔG = −n·F·ΔE. The reaction proceeds spontaneously from the pair with the lower (more negative) potential toward the pair with the higher potential.

A **diffusion potential** arises at the boundary between two solutions of different concentration or composition because the ions differ in mobility (for example, the mobile H^+^ runs ahead of Cl^−^). The **injury potential** between damaged and healthy tissue in the body is of this nature.

A **membrane potential** arises from the difference in ion concentrations on the two sides of a selectively permeable membrane. For a single ion it is calculated with the Nernst equation; for potassium at 37 °C: E~K~ = 61·lg([K^+^]~out~ / [K^+^]~in~) = 61·lg(4 / 140) ≈ −94 mV. The actual resting potential of the cell (≈ −70 mV) results from the contributions of several ions (K^+^, Na^+^, Cl^−^) and the work of Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase.

parts.text: The membrane potential is the basis of the work of excitable tissues. In **hyperkalemia**, [K^+^]~out~ rises and E~K~ becomes less negative — the cell depolarizes, sodium channels are inactivated and cardiac conduction is disturbed. ECG, EEG and EMG are based on recording the biopotentials of tissues.

blocks.text: A **galvanic cell** is a device that converts the chemical energy of a redox reaction into electrical energy. **The Daniell cell:** (−) Zn | ZnSO~4~ || CuSO~4~ | Cu (+). Oxidation occurs at the anode (Zn): Zn − 2e^−^ → Zn^2+^; reduction at the cathode (Cu): Cu^2+^ + 2e^−^ → Cu. Electromotive force: EMF = E~cathode~ − E~anode~ = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

blocks.text: **Potentiometry** is an analytical method based on measuring the potential of an indicator electrode (the EMF). **Direct potentiometry** (pH-metry, ionometry): pH = (E − E°) / 0.059. In **potentiometric titration** the equivalence point is found from a sharp jump in potential.

parts.text: A modern **blood gas analyzer** measures, in a single drop of blood within a few minutes, the pH with a glass electrode, pO~2~ and pCO~2~ with special electrodes, and Na^+^, K^+^ and Ca^2+^ with ion-selective electrodes. **Glucose meters** measure the current of a reaction involving glucose oxidase (amperometry).

blocks.text: The mitochondrial **respiratory chain** is an ordered series of redox pairs: electrons pass from NADH, which has a low standard potential, to oxygen, which has the highest. At each step part of the energy released is used to pump protons across the membrane and is then used for ATP synthesis.

blocks.text: **Calculation:** ΔE°′ = 0.82 − (−0.32) = 1.14 V; ΔG°′ = −n·F·ΔE°′ = −2 · 96 485 · 1.14 ≈ −220 000 J/mol = **−220 kJ/mol**. In theory this energy could form several ATP (≈ 30.5 kJ/mol each); in practice ≈ 2.5 ATP are synthesized when 1 pair of electrons passes from NADH to O~2~.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient has serum K^+^ = 7.0 mmol/L and tall, peaked T waves on the ECG. Take the intracellular potassium concentration as 140 mmol/L (37 °C).
cases.ask: How does the equilibrium potential of potassium change compared with normal (K^+^ = 4 mmol/L)? Explain the clinical significance.
cases.answer: Normally: E~K~ = 61·lg(4 / 140) ≈ −94 mV. In hyperkalemia: E~K~ = 61·lg(7 / 140) = 61·lg0.05 ≈ −79 mV. The membrane is less negative (depolarized), sodium channels are inactivated, and cardiac excitability and conduction are disturbed; there is a risk of asystole. Emergency treatment: calcium gluconate (stabilizes the membrane), insulin + glucose (moves K^+^ into the cells).

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient has a gold crown on one tooth and an amalgam (mercury–silver–tin alloy) filling in the neighboring tooth. He feels a metallic taste in the mouth and occasional “electric shocks”.
cases.ask: Explain the electrochemical cause of this phenomenon.
cases.answer: Saliva is an electrolyte solution; two metals with different standard potentials (gold — high, the tin of the amalgam — low) form a **galvanic cell** through the saliva (galvanism). The metal with the lower potential acts as the anode and corrodes, its ions pass into the saliva (metallic taste), and current flows when the metals touch. It is recommended to use identical or electrochemically compatible materials in the mouth.

topics.title: Surface phenomena and adsorption. Chromatography. Qualitative reactions based on adsorption. Quantitative assessment of adsorption

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of surface energy and surface tension, surface-active and surface-inactive substances, adsorption, desorption, absorption and chemisorption, the laws of adsorption on mobile and immobile surfaces (the Gibbs, Langmuir and Freundlich equations), and chromatographic methods and their significance in medicine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of surface energy, surface tension and surface activity;
surface-active, surface-inactive and surface-indifferent substances, and the Duclaux–Traube rule;
the difference between adsorption, absorption, desorption and chemisorption;
the Gibbs, Langmuir and Freundlich equations;
ion-exchange adsorption and the Paneth–Fajans rule;
the principles and types of chromatography and the R~f~ value.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the amount adsorbed from experimental data;
analyze an adsorption isotherm;
calculate R~f~ on a paper or thin-layer chromatogram;
justify the medical use of sorbents and surfactants.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Adsorption** is the accumulation of a substance on the **surface** of another phase; **absorption** is its uptake throughout the **volume**. Surface-active substances lower surface tension and are adsorbed positively at the surface (Γ > 0).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: A surfactant molecule — **“head in the water, tail in the air”**: the polar hydrophilic “head” (−COO^−^, −OH, −SO~3~^−^) sits in the water, the nonpolar hydrophobic hydrocarbon “tail” in the air or oil.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Activated charcoal also adsorbs drugs: drugs taken at the same time (contraceptives, antibiotics) become less effective. That is why other drugs are taken at least 1.5–2 hours before or after charcoal.

blocks.text: A molecule inside a phase is attracted equally from all sides, whereas a molecule at the surface is acted on by a resultant force directed inward. That is why the surface layer has excess energy — **surface energy**. The free surface energy per unit area is called **surface tension** (σ), J/m^2^ or N/m.

A system spontaneously tends to reduce its surface energy: drops take a spherical shape (the smallest surface), small drops merge into larger ones, and substances that lower σ accumulate at the surface. Water has a very high surface tension: ≈ 73 mN/m at 20 °C.

parts.text: **Hay’s test:** sulfur powder is sprinkled on the surface of urine. Normally the powder stays on the surface; if the urine contains bile acids (strong surfactants), surface tension falls and the powder sinks — the test is positive in obstructive jaundice and liver diseases.

items: **Surface-active substances (surfactants)** lower the surface tension of the solvent and accumulate at the surface: alcohols, carboxylic acids, soaps, bile acids, phospholipids, proteins. They have a **diphilic** (amphiphilic) structure.
**Surface-inactive substances** slightly raise the surface tension and move away from the surface into the bulk (negative adsorption): strong electrolytes (NaCl, KNO~3~), inorganic acids and alkalis.
**Surface-indifferent substances** hardly change the surface tension: glucose, sucrose.

blocks.text: **Surface activity** is the ability of a substance to lower surface tension: g = −dσ / dC. **The Duclaux–Traube rule:** in a homologous series, each CH~2~ group added to the hydrocarbon radical increases the surface activity **3–3.5 times** (formic < acetic < propionic < butyric acid).

parts.text: **Pulmonary surfactant** is a mixture of phospholipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and proteins that lines the inner surface of the alveoli. By Laplace’s law the collapsing pressure of an alveolus is P = 2σ / r; surfactant sharply lowers σ and prevents the alveoli from collapsing on expiration. When surfactant is lacking in preterm infants, **respiratory distress syndrome** develops; it is treated by giving natural or synthetic surfactant into the trachea.

blocks.text: **Sorption** is the uptake of one substance by another. The substance that takes up is the **sorbent** (adsorbent), and the substance taken up is the **sorbate** (adsorptive).

blocks.text: Adsorption is an **exothermic** process: as temperature rises, adsorption decreases and desorption increases. How much is adsorbed depends on the **specific surface area** of the sorbent: the inner pore surface of 1 g of activated charcoal reaches 500–1500 m^2^.

sections.title: 4. Adsorption on a mobile surface. The Gibbs equation

blocks.text: Liquid–gas and liquid–liquid boundaries are **mobile surfaces**. Adsorption of a solute at such a surface is described by the **Gibbs equation**: Γ = −(C / R·T)·(dσ / dC), where Γ is the surface excess (mol/m^2^).

items: If dσ / dC < 0 (surfactant), Γ > 0 — **positive adsorption**, the substance accumulates at the surface.
If dσ / dC > 0 (surface-inactive substance), Γ < 0 — **negative adsorption**, the substance moves from the surface into the bulk.

Surfactant molecules are **oriented** at the surface: as the concentration grows they stand upright and form a dense monomolecular layer (a “palisade”) — this is the physicochemical basis of the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane.

sections.title: 5. Adsorption on a solid surface. The Langmuir and Freundlich equations

blocks.text: **Langmuir’s theory of monomolecular adsorption:** adsorption occurs at the active sites of the sorbent; each site holds one molecule; when the surface is filled, a monomolecular layer is formed. **Langmuir equation:** Γ = Γ~∞~·K·C / (1 + K·C), where Γ~∞~ is the maximum (full-layer) adsorption and K is the adsorption constant.

items: At low concentration (K·C ≪ 1): Γ ≈ Γ~∞~·K·C — adsorption is proportional to concentration.
At high concentration (K·C ≫ 1): Γ ≈ Γ~∞~ — the surface is saturated.
**The empirical Freundlich equation** (for medium concentrations): x / m = K·C^1/n^; in logarithmic form lg(x / m) = lgK + (1 / n)·lgC — a straight line from which K and 1/n are found.

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Adsorption isotherm (by the Langmuir equation): a linear region at low concentration and saturation approaching Γ~∞~ at high concentration (left); the logarithmic form of the Freundlich equation (right) (drawn from calculated data).

blocks.text: **Quantitative assessment of adsorption:** after the sorbent is placed in a solution and equilibrium is reached, adsorption is found from the decrease in the concentration of the solution: Γ = (C~0~ − C)·V / m, where C~0~ and C are the initial and equilibrium concentrations, V the volume of solution and m the mass of sorbent.

sections.title: 6. Adsorption of electrolytes and ion exchange

blocks.text: **The Paneth–Fajans rule:** the surface of a crystal selectively adsorbs ions that are part of its lattice or isomorphous with them. For example, AgI crystals adsorb I^−^ in a solution with excess KI, and Ag^+^ with excess AgNO~3~ — this is how the charge of a colloidal particle arises (topic 8).

**Ion-exchange adsorption:** the sorbent gives one of its own ions to the solution and takes up an equivalent amount of another ion in its place. Such sorbents are called **ion exchangers**: **cation exchangers** (R−SO~3~H, exchange cations) and **anion exchangers** (R−N(CH~3~)~3~^+^OH^−^, exchange anions).

blocks.text: **Chromatography** is a method of separation and analysis based on the different distribution (selective adsorption) of the components of a mixture between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. It was discovered in 1903 by the Russian botanist **M.S. Tsvet**, who separated plant pigments in a column packed with chalk.

blocks.text: In paper and thin-layer chromatography the movement of a substance is described by the **R~f~ value**: R~f~ = l / L, where l is the distance from the start line to the spot of the substance and L is the distance from the start line to the solvent front. Under given conditions R~f~ is constant for each substance — the substance is identified by it.

parts.text: In medicine: **HPLC** — glycated hemoglobin (HbA~1c~), vitamins, drug concentrations in the blood; **gas chromatography** — ethanol in blood and urine, toxicological examination; **paper and TLC** — amino acids, screening for inherited aminoacidopathies (phenylketonuria); **gel filtration and affinity chromatography** — purification of proteins, antibodies and vaccines.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: In a study of the adsorption of methylene blue, 0.5 g of activated charcoal was added to 50 mL of a 0.002 M solution. After equilibrium the concentration fell to 0.0004 M.
cases.ask: Calculate the adsorption capacity of the charcoal (mmol/g). What does this experiment show for medicine?
cases.answer: Γ = (C~0~ − C)·V / m = (0.002 − 0.0004) · 0.05 / 0.5 = 0.0016 · 0.1 = 0.00016 mol/g = 0.16 mmol/g. 80 % of the dye passed onto the charcoal. Because of this property, activated charcoal binds toxins, alkaloids and drugs in the gastrointestinal tract — it is effective in acute oral poisoning if given early (within 1 hour).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: An infant born at week 29 of pregnancy develops shortness of breath, nasal flaring and chest retractions a few hours after birth. The X-ray shows a “ground-glass” appearance of the lungs.
cases.ask: What is the condition? What is its physicochemical basis and the principle of treatment?
cases.answer: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease). Pulmonary surfactant is produced in sufficient amounts only by about weeks 34–36 of pregnancy; in a preterm infant it is lacking, and surface tension in the alveoli remains high. By Laplace’s law (P = 2σ / r) small alveoli collapse on expiration (atelectasis). Treatment: surfactant preparation given into the trachea, respiratory support (CPAP); when there is a risk, glucocorticoids are given to the mother before delivery (they speed up surfactant synthesis).

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A blood sample from a newborn was examined by paper chromatography. The solvent front rose 12.0 cm above the start line, and a strong spot in the sample was located at 6.6 cm. Under these conditions the R~f~ of standard phenylalanine is 0.55.
cases.ask: Calculate the R~f~ of the spot. What may the result indicate?
cases.answer: R~f~ = 6.6 / 12.0 = 0.55 — it matches standard phenylalanine. A strong phenylalanine spot in the blood indicates that it is increased, that is, possible **phenylketonuria**. The diagnosis is confirmed by a quantitative method (tandem mass spectrometry or fluorimetry); treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet.

topics.title: Disperse systems

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the definition and classification of disperse systems, the methods of preparing and purifying colloidal solutions, the structure of a colloidal particle (micelle), the electrokinetic potential and electrokinetic phenomena, the molecular-kinetic and optical properties of colloidal systems, their stability and coagulation, coarse disperse systems and colloidal surfactants, and to link them with medicine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the dispersed phase and dispersion medium, and the classification of disperse systems;
the preparation of colloidal solutions by dispersion and condensation, dialysis and ultrafiltration;
the structure of the micelle, the thermodynamic and electrokinetic (ζ) potential;
electrophoresis and electroosmosis;
Brownian motion, diffusion, sedimentation and the Tyndall effect;
the stability of colloids, coagulation and the Schulze–Hardy rule.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the formula of a micelle for a given reaction;
assess the coagulating action of an electrolyte by the Schulze–Hardy rule;
distinguish colloidal systems from true solutions;
explain the clinical significance of the properties of disperse systems (ESR, dialysis, electrophoresis).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Particle size: true solution < **1 nm**, colloidal solution **1–100 nm**, coarse disperse system > **100 nm**. Colloids can be told apart from true solutions by the Tyndall effect (a cone of light).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The micelle “nesting doll”: **core → potential-determining ions → counterions of the adsorption layer → (granule) → counterions of the diffuse layer → (micelle)**. The micelle as a whole is electrically neutral; the granule is charged.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: By the Schulze–Hardy rule, coagulation is caused by the ion with a charge **opposite to that of the granule**, and its strength rises sharply with charge: for ions with charges 1 : 2 : 3 the coagulation thresholds are ≈ 730 : 11 : 1.

blocks.text: A **disperse system** is a heterogeneous system in which one substance (the **dispersed phase**) is distributed as small particles within another substance (the **dispersion medium**). The degree of division of the dispersed phase is expressed by its **dispersity** (D = 1 / a, where a is the particle size).
