blocks.text: According to the interaction between the dispersed phase and the medium, **lyophilic** systems (the particle interacts strongly with the solvent, forms spontaneously and is stable: solutions of proteins and starch) and **lyophobic** systems (weak interaction, a stabilizer is needed: metal sols, AgI sol) are distinguished.

sections.title: 2. Preparation and purification of colloidal solutions

items: **Dispersion methods** — breaking up large particles: mechanical (colloid mill), ultrasound, electric arc (Bredig’s method — metal sols), **peptization** (converting a precipitate into the colloidal state with an electrolyte or a surfactant).

**Condensation methods** — joining molecules and ions into particles: physical (solvent replacement — pouring an alcoholic solution of sulfur into water) and chemical (reduction, hydrolysis, exchange reactions): FeCl~3~ + 3H~2~O → Fe(OH)~3~ + 3HCl (in boiling water).

blocks.text: Colloidal solutions are purified from low-molecular impurities as follows: **dialysis** — passing ions and small molecules through a semipermeable membrane into pure solvent; **electrodialysis** — dialysis speeded up by an electric field; **ultrafiltration** — filtration through a membrane under pressure.

parts.text: **Hemodialysis (the “artificial kidney”)** is based on the principle of dialysis: the patient’s blood flows on one side of a semipermeable membrane and the dialysis solution on the other. Small molecules such as urea, creatinine and K^+^ pass into the solution, while proteins and blood cells stay in the blood. Fluid is removed by ultrafiltration. The **renal glomeruli** are a natural ultrafilter as well.

sections.title: 3. Structure of the colloidal particle (micelle). The electrokinetic potential

blocks.text: A particle of a lyophobic sol is a **micelle**. For example, when **excess KI** is added to AgNO~3~: AgNO~3~ + KI → AgI↓ + KNO~3~. According to the Paneth–Fajans rule, the AgI crystals (the core) adsorb the excess I^−^ ions from the solution.

Micelle formula: {[mAgI]·nI^−^·(n − x)K^+^}^x−^·xK^+^. Here [mAgI] is the **aggregate (core)**; nI^−^ are the **potential-determining ions**; (n − x)K^+^ are the counterions of the **adsorption layer**; {…}^x−^ is the **granule** (negatively charged); xK^+^ are the counterions of the **diffuse layer**.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Structure of a micelle of the AgI sol formed with excess KI: the core, the potential-determining I^−^ ions and the K^+^ counterions of the adsorption and diffuse layers (diagram).

blocks.text: The potential between the core surface and the solution is the **thermodynamic (φ) potential**; the potential at the slipping boundary between the granule and the diffuse layer is the **electrokinetic (ζ, zeta) potential**. The greater the ζ-potential, the more strongly the particles repel each other and the more stable the sol.

parts.text: If AgNO~3~ is in excess, the potential-determining ions are Ag^+^ and the granule is **positively** charged: {[mAgI]·nAg^+^·(n − x)NO~3~^−^}^x+^·xNO~3~^−^. That is, the sign of the charge depends on which reagent is in excess.

items: **Electrophoresis** — movement of particles of the dispersed phase in an external electric field toward the oppositely charged electrode.
**Electroosmosis** — movement of the dispersion medium (the liquid) through a porous barrier or capillary in an electric field.
**Streaming potential** — a potential difference that arises when a liquid is forced through a porous barrier under pressure (the reverse of electroosmosis).
**Sedimentation potential** (Dorn effect) — the potential arising while particles settle (the reverse of electrophoresis).

blocks.text: The rate of electrophoresis is proportional to the ζ-potential (the Helmholtz–Smoluchowski equation). The charge of proteins depends on pH: above the isoelectric point (pI) they are negatively charged, below it positively.

parts.text: Serum protein electrophoresis is widely used in diagnosis: in **multiple myeloma** a narrow “M-spike” appears in the γ region, in **nephrotic syndrome** albumin falls and α~2~ rises, in **liver cirrhosis** albumin falls and the γ-globulins rise broadly, and in **acute inflammation** α~1~ and α~2~ rise. In treatment, **electrophoresis** (delivery of drug ions through the skin) is used as a physiotherapy method.

items: **Brownian motion** — the random movement of colloidal particles under the impacts of the molecules of the medium; it keeps colloids from settling (kinetic stability).
**Diffusion** — the spontaneous spreading of particles from higher to lower concentration; in colloids it is much slower than in true solutions.
**Osmotic pressure** — very small in colloidal solutions because the number of particles is small (the oncotic pressure of plasma is ≈ 3.5–4 kPa).
**Sedimentation** — the settling of particles under gravity; it is accelerated in an ultracentrifuge and makes it possible to determine the molecular mass of proteins.

blocks.text: **Optical properties:** colloidal particles scatter light. When a beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution from the side, a bright cone is seen — the **Tyndall effect** (not seen in a true solution). By **Rayleigh’s law** scattering is inversely proportional to the 4th power of the wavelength — so short-wavelength blue light is scattered more strongly (why the sky looks blue). Colloidal particles are visible in the **ultramicroscope** and the electron microscope.

parts.text: The **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)** is based on the sedimentation property of blood as a disperse system: in inflammation fibrinogen and globulins increase, red cells stick together in “rouleaux” and settle faster. Normal values: men 2–10 mm/h, women 2–15 mm/h.

blocks.text: **Kinetic (sedimentation) stability** is the resistance of particles to settling (thanks to Brownian motion); **aggregative stability** is the resistance of particles to sticking together and growing. The factors of aggregative stability are the like charge of the particles (ζ-potential), the **solvate (hydrate) shell** and **protective colloids**.

**Coagulation** is the sticking together, growth and settling of colloidal particles. It is caused by temperature, stirring, adding an oppositely charged sol and, most often, **electrolytes**. The lowest concentration of an electrolyte needed to start coagulation is called the **coagulation threshold** (C~k~, mmol/L).

**The Schulze–Hardy rule:** coagulation is caused by the ion whose charge is opposite to that of the granule (the coagulating ion); its coagulating power is proportional to roughly the **6th power** of the charge. For singly, doubly and triply charged ions the thresholds are in the ratio 1 : (1/2)^6^ : (1/3)^6^ ≈ 730 : 11 : 1.

parts.text: **Protective colloids** (proteins, gelatin) coat the particles of a lyophobic sol and protect them from coagulation. In the blood, proteins keep particles of poorly soluble salts (calcium phosphate, cholesterol) in colloidal form; when this protective property weakens, **stone** formation becomes easier. Protargol and collargol are silver sols protected by protein.

sections.title: 7. Coarse disperse systems and colloidal surfactants

items: **Suspensions** — solid particles (> 100 nm) in a liquid: the BaSO~4~ contrast agent and many pediatric dosage forms; they are shaken before use.
**Emulsions** — one liquid as droplets in another: **direct** (oil in water, like milk) and **inverse** (water in oil, like butter). They are stabilized by **emulsifiers** (surfactants).
**Foams** and **aerosols** — disperse systems with gas; inhaled drugs are given as aerosols.

blocks.text: **Colloidal surfactants** (soaps, bile salts, phospholipids) above a certain concentration — the **critical micelle concentration** (CMC) — join into micelles: hydrophobic tails inside, hydrophilic heads outside. Water-insoluble substances (fats, cholesterol) “dissolve” inside the micelle — **solubilization**.

parts.text: In the intestine, **bile salts** emulsify fats into small droplets (increasing the surface on which lipase acts) and carry the products of fat digestion to the site of absorption as mixed micelles. When bile is lacking (obstructive jaundice), fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are not absorbed — **steatorrhea** develops. In parenteral nutrition, **lipid emulsions** stabilized with egg phospholipids are given intravenously.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: In the laboratory an iron(III) hydroxide sol was prepared by adding FeCl~3~ solution dropwise to boiling water. FeO^+^ ions are adsorbed on the particle surface, and the counterion is Cl^−^.
cases.ask: Write the formula of the micelle. Which of NaCl, Na~2~SO~4~ and Na~3~PO~4~ is needed in the smallest amount to coagulate the sol?
cases.answer: {[mFe(OH)~3~]·nFeO^+^·(n − x)Cl^−^}^x+^·xCl^−^ — the granule is positively charged. Coagulation is caused by anions; by the Schulze–Hardy rule the triply charged PO~4~^3−^ is the strongest, then SO~4~^2−^, and Cl^−^ the weakest. So **Na~3~PO~4~** is needed in the smallest amount (the thresholds are in roughly the reverse order of 1 : 11 : 730).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: Serum protein electrophoresis of a patient: albumin 38 %, α~1~ 4 %, α~2~ 8 %, β 10 %, and a narrow tall peak in the γ region (40 %). The patient complains of bone pain; ESR is 75 mm/h.
cases.ask: Interpret the electrophoretogram. Why is the ESR sharply increased?
cases.answer: The narrow tall peak in the γ region is a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-spike), typical of **multiple myeloma**; albumin is relatively reduced. The increase of large, positively charged proteins (paraprotein) in the plasma neutralizes the negative charge (ζ-potential) of the red cells; they stick together in “rouleaux” and settle quickly — the ESR rises sharply. The diagnosis is confirmed by immunofixation, Bence Jones protein in the urine and bone marrow examination.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with obstructive jaundice has pale, fatty, shiny stools, and the prothrombin time is prolonged.
cases.ask: Explain these signs using the properties of disperse systems and colloidal surfactants.
cases.answer: Because the bile duct is blocked, bile salts do not reach the intestine. As colloidal surfactants they emulsify fats and, by forming mixed micelles, solubilize fats and fat-soluble vitamins. Without bile, fat stays as large droplets and lipase acts poorly — **steatorrhea**; vitamin K is not absorbed and the liver synthesizes little prothrombin — blood clotting slows. Treatment: restore bile flow and give vitamin K parenterally.

goals.text: To teach the student the theory of the structure of organic compounds, isomerism and stereoisomerism, the electronic effects (inductive and mesomeric) that determine reactivity, the acidity and basicity of organic compounds, oxidation–reduction reactions, the classes of hydrocarbons and of compounds containing heteroatoms, and their medical significance.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: A.M. Butlerov’s theory of chemical structure;
structural and spatial isomerism, chirality, enantiomers, and D/L and R/S nomenclature;
inductive and mesomeric effects, conjugation and aromaticity;
the acidity and basicity of organic compounds according to Brønsted and Lewis;
the oxidation and reduction of alcohols, aldehydes and other compounds;
the classes of hydrocarbons and of compounds with the main functional groups.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the functional groups and the class of a compound;
find a chiral carbon atom and draw the enantiomers;
explain the effect of substituents on acidity and basicity by electronic effects;
link the oxidation of organic substances in the body (ethanol, methanol) with medical conditions.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Natural **amino acids belong to the L series**, natural **monosaccharides to the D series**. Enantiomers have the same physical properties, but their biological effects can be completely different (the thalidomide tragedy).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The oxidation ladder: **alcohol → aldehyde → acid → CO~2~** (primary alcohol); secondary alcohol → **ketone**. In the body: ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid (acetyl-CoA).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Methanol itself is not very toxic, but in the body it is oxidized to **formaldehyde** and **formic acid**: the optic nerve is damaged (blindness) and severe metabolic acidosis develops. The antidote is fomepizole or ethanol (they compete for alcohol dehydrogenase).

sections.title: 1. The theory of the structure of organic compounds

blocks.text: **Organic chemistry** is the chemistry of carbon compounds and their derivatives. More than 90 % of known substances are organic compounds; all biomolecules and most drugs belong to them.

items: The atoms in a molecule are joined in a definite **order** according to their valence; this order is called the **chemical structure** (A.M. Butlerov, 1861).
The properties of a substance depend not only on its composition but also on its **structure** — this is why **isomers** exist.
The atoms and groups of atoms in a molecule **influence each other**.
The structure can be deduced from the properties of a substance, and the properties from the structure.

blocks.text: In organic compounds the carbon atom is always **tetravalent**; it can be **sp^3^** (tetrahedral, 109.5°, alkanes), **sp^2^** (planar, 120°, alkenes, benzene, the carbonyl group) or **sp** (linear, 180°, alkynes) hybridized. Carbon atoms can form long chains and rings with each other — hence the endless variety of organic compounds.

blocks.text: **Chirality** is the property of a molecule of not being superimposable on its mirror image (like the right and left hands). Most often it is caused by an **asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom** with four different substituents. Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other are called **enantiomers**: they rotate the plane of polarized light by the same angle but in opposite directions; an equal mixture of them (a **racemate**) is optically inactive.

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: The enantiomers of alanine: L-alanine (S) and D-alanine (R) — mirror images of each other; the chiral center is the α-carbon atom (structural formulas drawn with RDKit).

blocks.text: **Nomenclature:** **D/L** — relative to glyceraldehyde (in the Fischer projection, OH or NH~2~ at the chiral center on the right — D, on the left — L); **R/S** — by the priority of the substituents (the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not enantiomers (for example, glucose and galactose).

parts.text: **The thalidomide tragedy** (1957–1961): the drug given to pregnant women as a sedative was a racemate; one enantiomer was sedative and the other **teratogenic**, and ≈ 10 000 children were born with limb defects (the enantiomers interconvert in the body). Today many drugs are produced as the active enantiomer: **levodopa** (L-DOPA), **levothyroxine**, **esomeprazole**, **levocetirizine**.

blocks.text: The distribution of electron density in a molecule determines its reactivity. The shift of electron density is described by two kinds of electronic effects.

items: **Inductive effect (I)** — a shift of electron density along a chain of σ-bonds; it fades quickly with distance. **−I**: electronegative atoms and groups withdraw electrons (F, Cl, OH, NH~2~, NO~2~, COOH). **+I**: alkyl groups donate electrons (CH~3~, C~2~H~5~).

**Mesomeric effect (M)** — a shift of electron density along a conjugated π-system; it is transmitted along the chain without fading. **+M**: groups with a lone pair donate electrons to the π-system (−OH, −NH~2~, −OR, halogens). **−M**: groups withdraw electrons from the π-system (C=O, COOH, NO~2~, C≡N).

blocks.text: **Conjugation** is the formation of one delocalized electron cloud by π-bonds, or by a π-bond and a lone pair; it lowers the energy of the molecule and increases its stability. **Aromaticity** (Hückel’s rule): a planar cyclic conjugated system with (4n + 2) π-electrons is especially stable — benzene (6 π-electrons), pyridine, pyrrole, the purine bases.

sections.title: 4. Acidity and basicity of organic compounds

blocks.text: **Brønsted theory:** an acid is a proton donor, a base is a proton acceptor. **Lewis theory:** an acid is an electron-pair acceptor, a base an electron-pair donor. By the type of acidic center, OH-, SH-, NH- and CH-acids are distinguished; the strength of an acid is determined by the stability of its conjugate base (anion).

blocks.text: **Basicity** is typical mainly of nitrogen compounds (the lone electron pair). Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia (+I effect): pK~a~ ≈ 10.6 for CH~3~NH~3~^+^ and 9.25 for NH~4~^+^. Aniline, however, is a very weak base (pK~a~ ≈ 4.6 for C~6~H~5~NH~3~^+^) because the nitrogen lone pair is conjugated with the benzene ring (+M).

parts.text: The degree of ionization of drugs determines their absorption: mainly the **un-ionized** form crosses membranes. Weak acids (aspirin, pK~a~ ≈ 3.5) are largely un-ionized in the acidic stomach and are partly absorbed there; weak bases (many alkaloids) are absorbed well in the more alkaline intestine. In poisoning, alkalinizing the urine speeds up the excretion of weak acids (salicylates, phenobarbital).

sections.title: 5. Oxidation and reduction of organic compounds

blocks.text: In organic chemistry **oxidation** is the addition of oxygen to a molecule or the removal of hydrogen, and **reduction** is the reverse. In the body these reactions are catalyzed by **dehydrogenases**; the hydrogen carriers are NAD^+^, NADP^+^ and FAD.

items: Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid: CH~3~CH~2~OH → CH~3~CHO → CH~3~COOH.
Secondary alcohol → ketone: CH~3~CH(OH)CH~3~ → CH~3~COCH~3~ (acetone).
Lactate ⇄ pyruvate (lactate dehydrogenase, NAD^+^/NADH).
Thiols are oxidized to disulfides: 2R−SH → R−S−S−R (cysteine → cystine, disulfide bridges in proteins).

parts.text: In the liver, ethanol is oxidized by **alcohol dehydrogenase** to acetaldehyde and then by **aldehyde dehydrogenase** to acetic acid. Accumulation of acetaldehyde causes facial flushing, nausea and palpitations — **disulfiram** blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, produces exactly this state, and is used to treat alcoholism.

blocks.text: **Crown ethers** are cyclic polyethers containing repeating −CH~2~−CH~2~−O− units. They were synthesized in 1967 by C. Pedersen (Nobel Prize in 1987 together with D. Cram and J.-M. Lehn). The oxygen atoms inside the ring surround a metal cation like a “crown” and form a strong complex.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2

items: **Selective binding:** the ring cavity must match the size of the cation: 12-crown-4 — Li^+^, 15-crown-5 — Na^+^, 18-crown-6 — K^+^.

**Ionophore action:** because the complex is hydrophobic on the outside, it carries the cation across a lipid membrane. Natural ionophores — the antibiotics **valinomycin** (K^+^) and **monensin** (Na^+^) — work on this principle and disturb the ion balance of the bacterial membrane.

**Prospects in medicine:** antimicrobial and antitumor effects are being studied; they are used in drug delivery, binding heavy metals and radionuclides, and making ion-selective electrodes (for measuring blood K^+^). Because crown ethers themselves are toxic, they are not yet widely used as clinical drugs.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient drank illegally sold “alcohol”. After 18 hours his vision became blurred and he had abdominal pain; blood pH 7.10, HCO~3~^−^ = 9 mmol/L.
cases.ask: What poisoning is suspected? Explain the chemical mechanism and the principle of treatment.
cases.answer: Methanol poisoning. Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase to **formaldehyde** and then by aldehyde dehydrogenase to **formic acid**. Formic acid causes severe metabolic acidosis and damages the mitochondria of the optic nerve (blindness). The delayed onset of symptoms is due to the time needed to form the metabolites. Treatment: **fomepizole** or ethanol (they occupy alcohol dehydrogenase competitively and stop methanol oxidation), sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis, folate.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: Levodopa (L-DOPA) is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; its D-enantiomer is ineffective.
cases.ask: Why do the enantiomers of one substance act differently in the body?
cases.answer: Enzymes, receptors and transport proteins are **chiral** structures built from L-amino acids; they bind the substrate at three points and, like a “hand in a glove”, recognize only one enantiomer. L-DOPA crosses the blood–brain barrier via the amino acid transporter and is converted to dopamine by L-aromatic amino acid decarboxylase; the D-form is not a substrate of this enzyme. That is why the drug is produced as the active enantiomer.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: In severe salicylate (pK~a~ ≈ 3) poisoning, the patient was given sodium bicarbonate and the urine pH was raised to 7.5–8.0.
cases.ask: Why does this measure speed up the excretion of salicylates?
cases.answer: Mainly the **un-ionized** molecule is reabsorbed across the membrane of the renal tubules. In alkaline urine the weak acid passes almost completely into the anion (the salicylate ion); the anion cannot cross the membrane and is “trapped” in the urine (ion trapping). As a result reabsorption decreases and excretion increases several-fold. This shows the medical significance of acidity.

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, properties and significance as metabolites and drugs of compounds that contain identical (polyfunctional) or different (heterofunctional) functional groups — polyhydric alcohols and phenols, polyamines, dicarboxylic acids, amino alcohols and catecholamines, hydroxy-, amino- and keto acids, and heterofunctional derivatives of benzene.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concept of poly- and heterofunctional compounds;
the properties and medical significance of glycerol, ethylene glycol, xylitol, sorbitol and mannitol;
polyhydric phenols and the quinone–hydroquinone redox system;
the significance of polyamines and dicarboxylic acids (oxalate, malonate, succinate, fumarate);
amino alcohols (ethanolamine, choline, acetylcholine) and catecholamines;
hydroxy and keto acids, and derivatives of salicylic and p-aminobenzoic acid.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the functional groups of a compound and classify it;
explain the detection of polyhydric alcohols by the qualitative reaction with Cu(OH)~2~;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A **polyfunctional** compound has identical functional groups (glycerol — 3 OH), a **heterofunctional** compound has different groups (lactic acid — OH and COOH; amino acids — NH~2~ and COOH). Most metabolites are heterofunctional.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The series of dicarboxylic acids (C~2~–C~5~): **“Oh My, Such Good”** — oxalic, malonic, succinic, glutaric.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Ethylene glycol** (antifreeze) tastes sweet but is highly toxic: in the body it is oxidized to glycolaldehyde, glyoxylic and **oxalic** acid — severe acidosis and kidney damage by calcium oxalate crystals result. The antidote is fomepizole or ethanol.

blocks.text: Alcohols are mono-, di- or polyhydric by the number of hydroxyl groups, and primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon that bears the OH. In **aromatic alcohols** the OH is attached not to the benzene ring but to a side chain (benzyl alcohol C~6~H~5~CH~2~OH); compounds with OH attached directly to the ring are called **phenols**.

items: **Ethanol** — its 70 % solution denatures proteins and has the strongest antiseptic action (96 % alcohol coagulates protein on the surface of microbes so quickly that it does not penetrate inside).
**Benzyl alcohol** — a preservative in injection solutions; toxic in newborns (“gasping syndrome”).
**Menthol** (a cyclic alcohol) — a cooling and distracting effect (validol, ointments).

blocks.text: **Qualitative reaction:** in an alkaline medium polyhydric alcohols dissolve the Cu(OH)~2~ precipitate and form a **deep blue** complex (copper glycerate) — monohydric alcohols do not give this reaction. This is due to the increased acidity of neighboring OH groups and the formation of a chelate.

**Polyhydric phenols:** pyrocatechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene), resorcinol (1,3-), hydroquinone (1,4-). The pyrocatechol residue is part of the **catecholamines**. Hydroquinone is easily oxidized to **quinone** and reduced back again: this reversible system is the basis of the work of **ubiquinone (coenzyme Q)** in the respiratory chain.

parts.text: In diabetes mellitus, during hyperglycemia glucose is reduced to sorbitol by **aldose reductase**. Sorbitol crosses membranes poorly and accumulates in the cells of the lens, nerves and kidneys, causing osmotic swelling — one mechanism of the development of **cataract, neuropathy and nephropathy**.

blocks.text: **Polyamines** are compounds with two or more amino groups. They are formed by decarboxylation of amino acids: **putrescine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~4~NH~2~ from ornithine and **cadaverine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~5~NH~2~ from lysine; **spermidine** and **spermine** are synthesized from putrescine.

items: At physiological pH polyamines carry several positive charges and bind to negatively charged **DNA and RNA**, stabilizing their structure; they are needed for cell division and growth.
Polyamines increase in rapidly dividing tissues and in **tumors**; inhibitors of the enzyme of their synthesis (ornithine decarboxylase), such as eflornithine, are used in treatment.
Putrescine and cadaverine are foul-smelling “cadaveric poisons” (ptomaines) formed when proteins putrefy.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A car-repair shop worker drank antifreeze by mistake. A few hours later he appeared drunk, and then metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15) developed; many crystals were found in the urine, and urine output decreased.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical basis of the poisoning. What crystals were found in the urine, and what is the treatment?
cases.answer: The **ethylene glycol** in antifreeze is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid → glyoxylic acid → **oxalic acid**. The acids cause acidosis; oxalate forms poorly soluble **calcium oxalate** crystals with Ca^2+^ and damages the renal tubules (acute kidney injury). Treatment: **fomepizole** or ethanol (they occupy alcohol dehydrogenase competitively), sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: After working with an organophosphate insecticide, a gardener was brought in with constricted pupils, heavy salivation and sweating, shortness of breath and muscle twitching.
cases.ask: What is the biochemical cause of the symptoms? Which drugs are given?
cases.answer: The organophosphate irreversibly phosphorylates the serine in the active site of **acetylcholinesterase**. Acetylcholine is not broken down and accumulates in the synapses, constantly stimulating muscarinic (miosis, salivation, bronchospasm) and nicotinic (muscle twitching, then paralysis) receptors. Treatment: **atropine** (blocks M-cholinergic receptors) in large doses, **oximes** that reactivate the enzyme (pralidoxime), respiratory support.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient took 15 g of paracetamol within 1 day for a headache. At first there are no symptoms except nausea.
cases.ask: What is the danger? Explain the chemical mechanism and the action of the antidote.
cases.answer: The danger is severe liver damage (fulminant hepatitis). At normal doses paracetamol is conjugated with glucuronic and sulfuric acids and excreted; at large doses these pathways become saturated and much toxic **NAPQI** is formed via cytochrome P450. NAPQI is normally neutralized by the SH group of **glutathione**; once glutathione is used up, it binds to hepatocyte proteins and causes necrosis (symptoms appear after 1–3 days). **N-acetylcysteine**, as a source of cysteine, restores glutathione synthesis; the earlier it is given, the more effective it is.

topics.title: Heterocyclic compounds as metabolites and drugs

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the structure, aromaticity and acid–base properties of five- and six-membered heterocycles with one or more heteroatoms and of bicyclic (fused) heterocycles, and of the important metabolites, vitamins, neurotransmitters and drugs derived from them.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification and naming of heterocycles;
the pyrrole, furan, thiophene, imidazole, pyrazole and thiazole rings and their derivatives;
the pyridine, pyrimidine and piperidine rings and their derivatives;
bicyclic systems such as indole, purine, quinoline and pteridine;
the difference between pyrrole and pyridine nitrogen, and lactim–lactam tautomerism;
heterocyclic neurotransmitters (serotonin, histamine, melatonin) and important drugs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify and name the heterocycle in the formula of a drug or metabolite;
assess the acid–base properties of a heterocycle from the type of nitrogen;
explain the clinical significance of purine metabolism and uric acid formation;
justify the action of antimetabolite drugs (5-fluorouracil, methotrexate, allopurinol) by their similarity to natural metabolites.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Pyrrole nitrogen** gives its lone pair to the aromatic sextet — it has almost no basic properties, and N−H is a weak acid. **Pyridine nitrogen** keeps its pair — a weak base (pK~a~ ≈ 5.2). **Imidazole** has both types of nitrogen — amphoteric, pK~a~ ≈ 7 (hence the buffer property of histidine).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“CUT the PY”**: Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine are PYrimidines; **“PURe As Gold”**: PURines are Adenine and Guanine. The reverse rule: the word **pyrimidine** is long but the ring is single; **purine** is short but has two rings.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Many powerful drugs are **antimetabolites** designed to resemble natural heterocyclic metabolites: 5-fluorouracil (uracil), 6-mercaptopurine (hypoxanthine), methotrexate (folate), allopurinol (hypoxanthine). They also act on rapidly dividing healthy cells — blood counts and mucous membranes must be monitored.

sections.title: 1. Classification of heterocyclic compounds. Five-membered rings with one heteroatom

blocks.text: **Heterocyclic compounds** are cyclic compounds whose ring contains, besides carbon, atoms of other elements (**heteroatoms**: N, O, S). They are classified by ring size (five-, six-membered), by the number and type of heteroatoms, and by the number of rings (monocyclic, fused). More than half of all drugs are heterocyclic compounds.

blocks.text: Pyrrole is aromatic: the π-electrons of the four carbons and the lone pair of nitrogen together form a sextet of 6 π-electrons. That is why the nitrogen pair of pyrrole gives no basic properties, while N−H is a weak acid (pK~a~ ≈ 17). Four pyrrole rings joined by methine bridges form the **porphine** ring.

parts.text: When heme is broken down, the pyrrole ring system opens and a linear tetrapyrrole — **bilirubin** — is formed. Its accumulation in the blood causes **jaundice**. **Phototherapy**, used to treat neonatal jaundice, converts bilirubin under blue light into water-soluble isomers and speeds up its excretion.

blocks.text: **Imidazole** has both types of nitrogen: one of the pyrrole type (N−H) and one of the pyridine type (basic). The pK~a~ of the imidazolium ion is ≈ 7.0 — very close to physiological pH. That is why histidine residues serve as **buffer** groups of proteins and as **proton carriers** in the active site of many enzymes (for example, serine proteases).

blocks.text: The nitrogen of **pyridine** does not give its lone pair to the aromatic system — it is a weak base (pK~a~ of the pyridinium ion ≈ 5.2). The pyridine ring is π-electron deficient: electrophilic substitution is difficult and nucleophilic attack is easy. **The active part of NAD^+^** is the pyridine ring of nicotinamide: it accepts a hydride ion (H^−^) and is reduced to NADH.

**Barbiturates** are derivatives of barbituric acid (pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione); they have hypnotic and anticonvulsant effects (phenobarbital). Barbituric acid itself is not pharmacologically active — two substituents at position 5 make it lipophilic and active.

blocks.text: **Lactim–lactam tautomerism:** in purines and pyrimidines with hydroxy groups (uracil, thymine, guanine, uric acid) a proton moves between oxygen and nitrogen: −N=C(OH)− ⇄ −NH−C(=O)−. Under physiological conditions the **lactam** (oxo) form predominates; it is this form that ensures correct hydrogen bonding between the bases in DNA. The rare lactim form can cause pairing errors — **point mutations**.

parts.text: **Uric acid** is the end product of purine metabolism in humans (xanthine oxidase: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid). Its solubility is low (pK~a~ ≈ 5.4); when it rises in the blood, sodium urate crystals deposit in the joints — **gout**. **Allopurinol** (an isomer of hypoxanthine) blocks xanthine oxidase and reduces uric acid formation.

items: **Serotonin** (5-hydroxytryptamine) — from tryptophan by hydroxylation and decarboxylation; mood, sleep, appetite, gut motility, platelet aggregation. Drugs that block its reuptake (fluoxetine, sertraline) are used to treat depression.
**Melatonin** — formed from serotonin in the pineal gland (at night); it regulates the circadian rhythm.

**Histamine** — from the decarboxylation of histidine; allergic reactions (H~1~), HCl secretion in the stomach (H~2~), a mediator. H~1~ blockers (loratadine) and H~2~ blockers (famotidine) are widely used.
**Caffeine** and **theophylline** (methylxanthines) — block adenosine receptors and inhibit phosphodiesterase: they stimulate the CNS and dilate the bronchi.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 52-year-old man woke up at night after an evening of meat dishes and beer with sudden pain, redness and swelling of the big toe joint. Blood uric acid is 560 μmol/L (normal in men 200–420).
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain it in terms of the chemical structure of uric acid and state the principle of long-term treatment.
cases.answer: **An attack of gout.** Uric acid is a purine derivative (2,6,8-trioxopurine), the end product of purine metabolism; the purines in meat and beer increase its formation, and alcohol reduces its renal excretion. Uric acid is poorly soluble; when its blood level exceeds the saturation limit, sodium urate crystals deposit in a joint (especially the cooler peripheral joints) and cause inflammation. Long-term treatment: **allopurinol** or febuxostat (block xanthine oxidase), limiting purine-rich food and alcohol, plenty of fluids.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with colon cancer was prescribed a course of 5-fluorouracil. During treatment mouth ulcers (stomatitis), diarrhea and a fall in white blood cells were observed.
cases.ask: How does the drug work, and why do these adverse effects occur?
cases.answer: 5-Fluorouracil is an antimetabolite of uracil (F instead of H at position 5). In the body it is converted to fluorodeoxyuridylate, which irreversibly blocks **thymidylate synthase**: thymidine nucleotides are not formed, DNA synthesis stops and rapidly dividing tumor cells die. However, rapidly dividing healthy cells — the mucosa of the mouth and intestine and the bone marrow — are also damaged: stomatitis, diarrhea and leukopenia are due to this. Blood counts are monitored during treatment.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A student with allergic rhinitis complains in spring of a blocked nose, sneezing and watery eyes. Loratadine was recommended.
cases.ask: What is the chemical mediator of the symptoms, how is it formed, and how does the drug act?
cases.answer: The mediator is **histamine**: it is formed in mast cells by decarboxylation of histidine (histidine decarboxylase) and released on contact with the allergen. It is a biogenic amine with an imidazole ring that stimulates **H~1~ receptors**, increasing vascular permeability (swelling, nasal congestion) and irritating sensory nerves (itching, sneezing). Loratadine is an H~1~ receptor blocker; it prevents histamine from binding to the receptor.

the pyranose and furanose forms, α- and β-anomers, and mutarotation;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A disaccharide is **reducing** if one of its monosaccharides still has a **free hemiacetal (glycosidic) hydroxyl** (maltose, lactose). In sucrose both anomeric hydroxyls are used up in the bond — it is **non-reducing**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Disaccharides: **“Mal-Glu-Glu, Lac-Gal-Glu, Suc-Glu-Fru”** — maltose = glucose + glucose, lactose = galactose + glucose, sucrose = glucose + fructose.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Humans have no enzyme that breaks down **cellulose** (β-1,4-glycosidase): it is not digested, but as **dietary fiber** it stimulates gut motility and binds cholesterol and bile acids. Starch, on the other hand, has α-1,4 bonds and is easily broken down by amylase.

blocks.text: **Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxycarbonyl compounds and their derivatives; most have the general formula C~n~(H~2~O)~m~. They provide ≈ 50–60 % of dietary energy and are the main energy source; the brain and red blood cells use almost only glucose.

items: **By the carbonyl group:** aldoses (aldehyde group — glucose, galactose, ribose) and ketoses (keto group — fructose, ribulose).
**By the number of carbons:** trioses (glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone), tetroses, pentoses (ribose, deoxyribose, xylose), hexoses (glucose, galactose, mannose, fructose).
**The D and L series** are defined by the configuration of the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group (C-5 in hexoses); natural monosaccharides belong mainly to the **D series**.

blocks.text: An aldohexose has 4 chiral carbons, so 2^4^ = 16 stereoisomers (8 pairs of enantiomers) exist. Diastereomers that differ at only one chiral center are called **epimers**: D-glucose and D-galactose are **C-4** epimers, D-glucose and D-mannose are **C-2** epimers.

In solution monosaccharides exist mainly in **cyclic** form: the carbonyl group forms an intramolecular hemiacetal with a hydroxyl of the same molecule. A six-membered ring is a **pyranose**, a five-membered one a **furanose**. The new chiral center that appears when the ring closes (C-1) is the **anomeric** center: OH below the plane of the ring (in the Haworth formula) — the **α**-anomer, above — the **β**-anomer.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old student complains of bloating, pain and loose stools 1–2 hours after drinking milk. He tolerates kefir and cheese well.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the chemical mechanism.
cases.answer: **Lactase deficiency** (lactose intolerance). Lactose is a disaccharide of galactose and glucose with a β-1,4-glycosidic bond; it is broken down by **lactase** (β-galactosidase) of the small intestinal mucosa. When the enzyme is lacking, lactose is not absorbed; being osmotically active, it draws water into the intestine (diarrhea), and in the large intestine bacteria ferment it into gases (H~2~, CO~2~, CH~4~) and acids (bloating, pain). In kefir and cheese lactose has been partly broken down by bacteria, so they are well tolerated.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus has fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L and HbA~1c~ = 8.5 %.
cases.ask: How is HbA~1c~ formed and what does it show? Which property of carbohydrates is involved?
cases.answer: The open (aldehyde) form of glucose condenses non-enzymatically with the amino group of the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain (Schiff base → Amadori rearrangement) — **glycated hemoglobin** is formed. The reaction depends on blood glucose concentration and time, and since red cells live ≈ 120 days, HbA~1c~ reflects the mean glycemia over the last 2–3 months. 8.5 % means the diabetes is poorly controlled (the target is usually < 7 %); treatment should be adjusted.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with deep vein thrombosis was given heparin. A few hours later signs of bleeding appeared.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical structure and mechanism of action of heparin. How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: Heparin is a highly sulfated glycosaminoglycan built from glucosamine and uronic acids; it is the most strongly negatively charged biomolecule. Through a specific pentasaccharide sequence it binds to **antithrombin III** and increases a thousandfold the rate at which antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — blood clotting slows. The antidote is the positively charged protein **protamine sulfate**: it forms an electrostatic complex with heparin and neutralizes it.

topics.title: Amino acids. Peptides and proteins. Structure and properties

goals.text: To teach the student the concept of biopolymers and bioregulators, the structure, classification, physicochemical properties and biological functions of α-amino acids, the peptide bond and biologically active peptides, the primary and spatial structure, classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins, and to develop the skills of performing qualitative reactions of amino acids and determining serum protein by the biuret method.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure of proteinogenic amino acids, their classification by side chain, and the essential amino acids;
the amphoteric nature of amino acids, the zwitterion and the isoelectric point;
the chemical reactions and biological functions of amino acids;
the structure of the peptide bond and biologically active peptides;
the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of proteins;
the classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform the qualitative reactions of amino acids and proteins and explain the result;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In blood serum **total protein is 65–85 g/L** and albumin 35–50 g/L. The **biuret reaction** detects at least two peptide bonds — that is why free amino acids and dipeptides do not give this reaction.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The 8 essential amino acids for adults: **“Very Lazy Ice Tigers Meet Lions For Tea”** — Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Threonine, Methionine, Lysine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan; histidine is also essential for children.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: At its **isoelectric point** (pI) a protein has zero net charge, its lowest solubility and does not move in an electric field. Protein precipitation and separation by electrophoresis are based on this very property.

sections.title: 1. The concept of biopolymers and bioregulators

blocks.text: **Biopolymers** are natural high-molecular compounds built from monomers: **proteins** (monomer — α-amino acids), **nucleic acids** (nucleotides) and **polysaccharides** (monosaccharides). **Bioregulators** are substances that control the activity of cells and organs in small amounts: hormones, neurotransmitters, vitamins, regulatory peptides, prostaglandins.

sections.title: 2. Structure and classification of α-amino acids

blocks.text: Proteins contain 20 **α-amino acids**; their general formula is H~2~N−CH(R)−COOH. In all of them except glycine (R = H) the α-carbon is chiral, and natural amino acids belong to the **L series**. They differ from each other only in the side chain (R).

blocks.text: Amino acids that are not synthesized in the body and must come with food are called **essential**: in adults — valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan; in the growing organism — also histidine (and partly arginine).

sections.title: 3. Physical and chemical properties of amino acids

blocks.text: Amino acids are **amphoteric**: −COOH gives acidic and −NH~2~ basic properties. In solution and in crystals they exist as a **zwitterion** (dipolar ion): ^+^H~3~N−CH(R)−COO^−^. That is why they dissolve well in water, melt (decompose) at high temperature and dissolve poorly in organic solvents.

The **isoelectric point** (pI) is the pH at which an amino acid has zero net charge: for neutral amino acids pI = (pK~1~ + pK~2~) / 2. For example, for glycine pK~1~ (COOH) = 2.34 and pK~2~ (NH~3~^+^) = 9.60, so pI = 5.97. At pH < pI the amino acid is positively charged, at pH > pI negatively charged.

parts.text: **Phenylketonuria** is an inherited deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase: phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine, accumulates in the blood and disturbs brain development (intellectual disability). Newborns are screened; treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet. **Homocystinuria, alkaptonuria and maple syrup urine disease** are other aminoacidopathies.

blocks.text: The −CO−NH− bond formed with loss of water between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another is called the **peptide bond**. It has partial double-bond character (C−N mesomerism), so it is **planar** and rotation around it is restricted; in peptides it is mostly in the **trans** configuration. A peptide chain has a free amino group at its start (**N-terminus**) and a free carboxyl at its end (**C-terminus**).

blocks.text: The spatial structure of a protein, and hence its function, is **determined by its primary structure** (C. Anfinsen’s experiment). An example of quaternary structure is **hemoglobin** (2 α- and 2 β-chains, α~2~β~2~): the protomers interact when binding oxygen (cooperativity).

parts.text: **Sickle cell anemia:** at position 6 of the hemoglobin β-chain **glutamate is replaced by valine** (HbS). This single change in the primary structure creates a hydrophobic “sticky” patch in the deoxy form; the molecules polymerize, red cells take a sickle shape and block the capillaries. In **prion diseases**, on the other hand, the primary structure of the protein is unchanged, but its secondary structure switches from α-helix to β-sheet.

sections.title: 7. Classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins

items: **Simple proteins** — consist only of amino acids: albumins, globulins, histones, protamines, scleroproteins (collagen, keratin, elastin).
**Conjugated proteins** — protein + prosthetic group: glycoproteins, lipoproteins, nucleoproteins, chromoproteins (hemoglobin), phosphoproteins (casein), metalloproteins (ferritin).

**Functions:** catalytic (enzymes), structural (collagen), transport (hemoglobin, albumin), protective (immunoglobulins, fibrinogen), regulatory (insulin), contractile (actin, myosin), receptor, storage (ferritin, casein).

blocks.text: The molecular mass of proteins ranges from ≈ 6 000 (insulin ≈ 5 800) to several million daltons. It is determined by **ultracentrifugation** (sedimentation constant, Svedberg unit), **gel filtration**, **electrophoresis** (with sodium dodecyl sulfate) and mass spectrometry.

Protein solutions are **lyophilic colloids**: the particles are 1–100 nm, they give the Tyndall effect, do not pass through membranes and are highly viscous. Their stability has two factors — **charge** and the **hydration shell**. Removing them precipitates the protein: **salting out** (ammonium sulfate — reversible; globulins precipitate at half saturation, albumins at full saturation), **isoelectric precipitation**, **denaturation** (heating, strong acids and alkalis, heavy-metal salts, alcohol — the spatial structure is destroyed, often irreversibly).

parts.text: In poisoning with salts of heavy metals (mercury, lead, copper), **milk** or **egg white** is given as emergency first aid: the proteins form insoluble compounds with the metal ions, bind them in the gut and reduce their absorption; then the stomach is washed out.

blocks.text: Determination of total serum protein by the biuret method

**Principle of the method:** in an alkaline medium the peptide bonds of protein form a violet complex with Cu^2+^; the color intensity (optical density at 540 nm) is proportional to the protein concentration.

items: Prepare three tubes: test (0.1 mL serum), standard (0.1 mL of 70 g/L albumin solution) and blank (0.1 mL of 0.9 % NaCl).
Add 5 mL of biuret reagent to each and mix.
Leave at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Measure the optical density against the blank on a photoelectric colorimeter with a green filter (540 nm).
Calculate: C = (E~test~ / E~standard~) · C~standard~ (g/L).

parts.text: **Hypoproteinemia** (< 65 g/L) occurs in starvation, liver cirrhosis (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome and burns (loss); oncotic pressure falls and **edema** appears. **Hyperproteinemia** (> 85 g/L) occurs in dehydration (relative) and multiple myeloma (paraprotein).

blocks.text: Study of the physicochemical properties of proteins

items: **Salting out:** add an equal volume of saturated (NH~4~)~2~SO~4~ to egg white solution — the globulins precipitate; saturate the filtrate with crystalline salt — the albumins precipitate. When water is added the precipitate dissolves again (a reversible process).
**Denaturation by heating:** boil the protein solution — turbidity and clots appear; they do not dissolve on cooling.
**Precipitation by heavy metals:** add drops of CuSO~4~ or lead acetate to the protein solution — a precipitate forms.
**With acids:** carefully layer protein solution over conc. HNO~3~ — a white ring forms at the boundary (Heller’s test — detection of protein in urine).

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: Serum protein of a patient was determined by the biuret method. For the standard albumin solution (70 g/L) E = 0.35, for the serum E = 0.24. The patient has edema of the legs and face and 6 g of protein in the urine per day.
cases.ask: Calculate the total protein. Explain the mechanism of the edema.
cases.answer: C = (0.24 / 0.35) · 70 = 48 g/L — **hypoproteinemia** (normal 65–85 g/L). Heavy loss of protein (mainly albumin) in the urine is typical of **nephrotic syndrome**. Albumin creates most of the oncotic pressure of plasma; when it falls, water passes from the capillaries into the interstitial space — **oncotic edema** appears.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: The pK values of glutamic acid are: α-COOH 2.19; γ-COOH 4.25; α-NH~3~^+^ 9.67. Electrophoresis is carried out at pH 7.0.
cases.ask: Find the isoelectric point of glutamic acid and say toward which electrode it moves at pH 7.0.
cases.answer: For an acidic amino acid pI is the mean of the pK values of the two acidic groups: pI = (2.19 + 4.25) / 2 = 3.22. pH 7.0 > pI, so glutamate has a net **negative** charge (both carboxyls ionized, the amino group protonated: net charge −1) and moves toward the **anode (+)**.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A chemical plant worker accidentally swallowed some mercury(II) chloride solution. Before the ambulance arrived, a colleague gave him 3 raw egg whites mixed together to drink.
cases.ask: What is the chemical basis of this measure?
cases.answer: Heavy-metal ions such as mercury bind to the SH, carboxyl and imidazole groups of proteins, **denature** them and form insoluble metal–protein compounds (a precipitate). The proteins of egg white (ovalbumin) bind the Hg^2+^ ions in the stomach and reduce their interaction with the proteins of the mucosa and their absorption. Then the stomach is washed out and specific antidotes (unithiol, dimercaprol) are given.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Nucleoside** = nitrogenous base + pentose (N-glycosidic bond); **nucleotide** = nucleoside + phosphate (phosphoester bond). In DNA A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds); the strands are **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: RNA is easily hydrolyzed by alkali (because of the 2′-OH group of ribose), while DNA is resistant to alkali — that is why DNA is the more stable molecule for storing hereditary information. In acid, on the other hand, the **purine bases** are released from DNA first.

sections.title: 1. Structure and properties of nucleosides and nucleotides

blocks.text: A **nucleoside** is a purine or pyrimidine base joined to ribose or 2′-deoxyribose by a **β-N-glycosidic bond**: atom N-9 of purines or N-1 of pyrimidines is bound to atom C-1′ of the pentose. A **nucleotide** is a phosphate ester of a nucleoside (most often at the 5′-OH).

blocks.text: Because of the phosphate residue, nucleotides are **acidic** and negatively charged at physiological pH. The N-glycosidic bond is hydrolyzed in acid (more easily in purines than in pyrimidines). The aromatic rings of the bases absorb ultraviolet light strongly at **260 nm** — the spectrophotometric determination of nucleic acids is based on this.

parts.text: Many antiviral drugs are **chain terminators**: they are added to DNA as nucleotides, but because they lack the 3′-OH group to which the next nucleotide is attached, chain elongation stops.

sections.title: 3. Nucleoside polyphosphates. High-energy bonds. Cyclic nucleotides

blocks.text: One or two more phosphate residues may be attached to the 5′-phosphate of a nucleotide by **phosphoanhydride** bonds: AMP → ADP → ATP. Bonds whose hydrolysis releases much energy (ΔG°′ < −25 kJ/mol) are called **high-energy (macroergic)** and are shown with the sign “∼”: A−P∼P∼P.

items: ATP + H~2~O → ADP + P~i~; ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol.
ATP + H~2~O → AMP + PP~i~; ΔG°′ = −45.6 kJ/mol (pyrophosphate is then hydrolyzed, making the reaction irreversible).
Reasons for the high energy: mutual repulsion of the negative charges of the phosphate residues, resonance stabilization and stronger hydration of the products.
Other high-energy compounds: GTP, UTP, CTP, creatine phosphate, phosphoenolpyruvate, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, acetyl-CoA.

blocks.text: **Cyclic nucleotides:** **cAMP** (3′,5′-cyclic AMP) is formed from ATP by **adenylate cyclase** and acts as a **second messenger** that carries the effect of hormones such as epinephrine and glucagon into the cell; it is broken down to AMP by phosphodiesterase. **cGMP** is formed by guanylate cyclase (activated by NO) and relaxes smooth muscle.

parts.text: **Caffeine and theophylline** block phosphodiesterase and slow the breakdown of cAMP (bronchodilation, CNS stimulation). **Sildenafil** blocks type 5 phosphodiesterase, which breaks down cGMP. **Cholera toxin** permanently activates adenylate cyclase: cAMP rises sharply in intestinal cells and Cl^−^ and water are lost — severe diarrhea.

blocks.text: The active part of NAD^+^ is atom C-4 of the nicotinamide ring: it accepts a **hydride ion** (H^−^) from the substrate and becomes NADH, while the second proton goes into solution: NAD^+^ + 2H → NADH + H^+^. NADH absorbs light at 340 nm (NAD^+^ does not) — many enzyme activities (ALT, AST, LDH) are measured this way. FAD adds two hydrogen atoms at atoms N-1 and N-5 of the isoalloxazine ring.

sections.title: 5. The polynucleotide chain. Primary and spatial structure of nucleic acids

blocks.text: Nucleotides join through **3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds** to form a polynucleotide chain: the 3′-OH of the pentose of one nucleotide binds to the 5′-phosphate of the next. One end of the chain has a free 5′-phosphate and the other a free 3′-OH; the sequence is written in the **5′→3′** direction. The nucleotide sequence is the **primary structure** of a nucleic acid.

blocks.text: **The DNA double helix** (J. Watson and F. Crick, 1953): two **antiparallel** strands are twisted to the right around a common axis; the bases are inside and the phosphate–sugar backbone outside. The bases pair **complementarily**: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). In the B form there are ≈ 10 base pairs per turn, the pitch is 3.4 nm and the diameter 2 nm. The helix is held by hydrogen bonds and base **stacking** interactions.

parts.text: **Chargaff’s rules:** in DNA A = T and G = C; the number of purines equals the number of pyrimidines. DNA rich in G–C pairs is more stable (three hydrogen bonds) and “melts” at a higher temperature.

sections.title: 6. Hydrolysis of nucleic acids. Denaturation, renaturation and hybridization. DNA synthesis

items: **Acid hydrolysis:** in weak acid the purine bases are released first (apurinic DNA); complete hydrolysis gives nitrogenous bases, pentose and phosphoric acid.
**Alkaline hydrolysis:** RNA is broken down through 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotides into 2′- and 3′-nucleotides; DNA is resistant.
**Enzymatic hydrolysis:** nucleases — DNase, RNase (endo- and exonucleases); **restriction enzymes** cut DNA at specific sequences (genetic engineering).

blocks.text: **Denaturation (“melting”):** heating, alkali or urea break the hydrogen bonds and the double helix separates into two strands; absorbance at 260 nm rises by 30–40 % (the **hyperchromic effect**). The temperature at which half the strands separate is the **melting temperature** (T~m~); it rises with the G–C content. On slow cooling the complementary strands rejoin — **renaturation** (annealing). The joining of complementary strands from different sources is **hybridization** (DNA–DNA, DNA–RNA).

**DNA synthesis (replication)** is **semiconservative**: each new molecule consists of one old and one new strand (the Meselson–Stahl experiment). DNA polymerase synthesizes the new strand only in the **5′→3′** direction, starting from an RNA primer, from deoxynucleoside triphosphates; the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments that are joined by ligase.

parts.text: Denaturation and hybridization underlie the **polymerase chain reaction** (PCR): denaturation at 94–95 °C, primer annealing at 50–65 °C, and chain extension at 72 °C by heat-stable Taq polymerase. In 30–35 cycles a DNA fragment is copied billions of times — it is used for infections (COVID-19, tuberculosis, HIV), hereditary diseases and forensic examination.

blocks.text: The chemical causes of mutations are changes in the structure of the bases (deamination, alkylation, oxidation), mispairing due to wrong tautomeric forms (lactim, imino) and physical damage to the strand. The cell has many **repair** systems; inherited defects in them (for example, **xeroderma pigmentosum**) sharply increase the tendency to cancer.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A fragment of one DNA strand: 5′-ATGGCTAACG-3′.
cases.ask: Write the complementary strand. Check the base composition of the fragment by Chargaff’s rule and write the mRNA sequence synthesized from this fragment (if this strand is the template).
cases.answer: Complementary strand: 3′-TACCGATTGC-5′ (in the 5′→3′ direction: 5′-CGTTAGCCAT-3′). In the double-stranded fragment (20 bases): A = T = 5, G = C = 5 — consistent with Chargaff’s rule. If the given strand is the template, the mRNA is complementary to it and contains uracil instead of thymine: 5′-CGUUAGCCAU-3′.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with HIV infection was prescribed zidovudine (3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine).
cases.ask: How does the drug work? Explain in terms of its chemical structure.
cases.answer: Zidovudine is a thymidine analog: an azido group (−N~3~) replaces the 3′-OH of deoxyribose. In the cell it is phosphorylated to the triphosphate and incorporated into the DNA chain in place of dTMP by the viral **reverse transcriptase**. Because there is no 3′-OH to attach the next nucleotide, no phosphodiester bond can form — **the chain is terminated** and viral DNA is not synthesized. Reverse transcriptase uses zidovudine much more readily than human DNA polymerases, which ensures selective action.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with cholera has up to 10–15 L a day of “rice-water” diarrhea and severe dehydration.
cases.ask: Explain the molecular mechanism of the disease in terms of cyclic nucleotides.
cases.answer: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein that controls **adenylate cyclase** in the intestinal epithelium and leaves it permanently active. As a result **cAMP** is formed from ATP continuously; via protein kinase A, cAMP activates the CFTR chloride channels — Cl^−^, Na^+^ and a lot of water pour into the intestinal lumen. The basis of treatment is rehydration with oral or intravenous water–electrolyte (glucose–salt) solutions, plus antibiotics.

sections.title: 1. Classification of lipids. The saponification reaction

blocks.text: **Lipids** are natural compounds that are insoluble in water and soluble in nonpolar organic solvents (ether, chloroform, benzene). They serve as an energy store (1 g of fat — 38.9 kJ), as components of membranes, as thermal and mechanical protection, and as precursors of hormones, vitamins and signal molecules.

blocks.text: **Saponification** is the hydrolysis of ester bonds in the presence of an alkali: triglyceride + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3R−COONa (soap). Sodium salts are hard soaps, potassium salts liquid soaps. Nonsaponifiable lipids have no ester bond and are not broken down by alkali.

Natural fatty acids are usually unbranched monocarboxylic acids with an **even number** (C~14~–C~24~) of carbon atoms. Shorthand: C18:2 means 18 carbons and 2 double bonds; the **ω** (n) number shows the position of the first double bond counted from the methyl end.

blocks.text: A cis double bond creates a “kink” in the chain and prevents tight packing of the molecules — that is why vegetable **oils**, rich in unsaturated acids, are **liquid**, and animal **fats**, rich in saturated acids, are **solid**. Unsaturated fatty acids in membranes provide their fluidity.

sections.title: 3. Mono-, di- and triglycerides. Chemical properties of fats

blocks.text: **Acylglycerols** are esters of glycerol with fatty acids: mono-, di- and **triglycerides** (triacylglycerols). If all three acyl residues are the same, the triglyceride is **simple** (tripalmitin); if they differ, it is **mixed**; natural fats consist mainly of mixed triglycerides.

parts.text: **Lipid peroxidation** (LPO) proceeds as a chain reaction in the polyunsaturated fatty acids of membranes under the action of reactive oxygen species; its product is malondialdehyde. It increases in atherosclerosis, ischemic injury, aging and inflammation. Protection comes from antioxidants: **vitamin E** (tocopherol), vitamin C, glutathione and selenium-containing glutathione peroxidase.

blocks.text: **Nutritional value of fats:** fats should provide ≈ 25–30 % of dietary energy; they are a source of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and of the **essential fatty acids** (linoleic, α-linolenic — formerly called “vitamin F”). Their deficiency leads to dermatitis, growth retardation and slow wound healing.

**Glycerophospholipids** are derivatives of phosphatidic acid: fatty acids at positions 1 and 2 of glycerol, and at position 3 a phosphate with an amino alcohol or another group attached to it. They are **diphilic** molecules: two hydrophobic “tails” and a polar “head” — that is why in water they form the lipid bilayer (membrane) and liposomes.

blocks.text: **L-Glycerol 3-phosphate is formed in the body in two ways:** 1) phosphorylation of glycerol by ATP (**glycerol kinase**, mainly in the liver and kidney): glycerol + ATP → L-glycerol 3-phosphate + ADP; 2) reduction of the glycolytic intermediate dihydroxyacetone phosphate (**glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase**, NADH): dihydroxyacetone phosphate + NADH + H^+^ → L-glycerol 3-phosphate + NAD^+^ (in adipose tissue and muscle). Triglycerides and phospholipids are synthesized from it.

**Sphingolipids** contain the 18-carbon amino alcohol **sphingosine** instead of glycerol. When the amino group of sphingosine forms an amide bond with a fatty acid, a **ceramide** results; ceramide joined with phosphocholine is **sphingomyelin** (the myelin sheath of nerve fibers).

items: **Cerebrosides** (galactocerebrosides) — ceramide + one galactose (or glucose); abundant in myelin and nervous tissue.
**Gangliosides** — ceramide + an oligosaccharide containing sialic (N-acetylneuraminic) acid; in nerve cell membranes, with receptor and cell–cell recognition functions.
**Sulfatides** — sulfated cerebrosides.

parts.text: **Sphingolipidoses** are inherited deficiencies of the lysosomal enzymes that break down sphingolipids: **Gaucher disease** (glucocerebrosidase — glucocerebroside accumulates; enzyme replacement therapy exists), **Tay–Sachs disease** (hexosaminidase A — GM~2~ ganglioside accumulates in brain neurons), **Niemann–Pick disease** (sphingomyelinase).

blocks.text: **Terpenes** are compounds built from **isoprene** (C~5~H~8~) units. They are divided into monoterpenes (C~10~: menthol, camphor, limonene), sesquiterpenes (C~15~), diterpenes (C~20~: retinol), triterpenes (C~30~: squalene — the precursor of cholesterol) and tetraterpenes (C~40~: carotenoids). In the body isoprenoids are synthesized from acetyl-CoA by the **mevalonate** pathway.

items: **β-Carotene** is split in two in the intestinal wall to give two molecules of **vitamin A** (retinal); carrots, pumpkin, apricots.
**Lycopene** (tomatoes), **lutein** and **zeaxanthin** (the macula of the retina) are antioxidants.
Vitamin A (retinol) is part of the visual pigment **rhodopsin** and controls epithelial differentiation; its deficiency causes “night blindness” (hemeralopia) and xerophthalmia.

parts.text: **Statins** (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) block **HMG-CoA reductase**, the key enzyme of the mevalonate pathway, and reduce cholesterol synthesis in the liver — LDL cholesterol falls; they are the main drug group for preventing atherosclerosis and its complications (myocardial infarction, stroke).

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old man who smokes and is overweight. Blood lipid profile: total cholesterol 7.1 mmol/L, LDL cholesterol 4.9 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 0.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Interpret the results. What chemically based dietary advice would you give, and which drug group may be used?
cases.answer: All values are atherogenic: total cholesterol (> 5.2), LDL (> 3.0) and triglycerides (> 1.7) are raised and HDL (< 1.0) is lowered — **atherogenic dyslipidemia** with a high risk of cardiovascular disease. Advice: reduce saturated and especially **trans fats** (margarine, fried fast food), replace them with **ω-3** (fish, flaxseed oil) and monounsaturated (olive oil) fats, eat more fiber, stop smoking and lose weight. Drug: **statins** (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: In the laboratory, 1 mol of tripalmitin (M = 807 g/mol) was completely saponified with sodium hydroxide.
cases.ask: Write the reaction equation. How many moles of NaOH are used, and how many grams of sodium palmitate (M = 278 g/mol) are formed?
cases.answer: Tripalmitin + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3C~15~H~31~COONa. **3 mol of NaOH** are needed for 1 mol of triglyceride; 3 mol of sodium palmitate are formed: m = 3 · 278 = 834 g. In addition, 1 mol (92 g) of glycerol is released.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A 9-month-old breast-fed baby who spends most of the winter indoors has sweating, a bald patch on the back of the head, softening of the skull bones and a “rachitic rosary”. Blood phosphate is reduced and alkaline phosphatase is raised.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its chemical basis in terms of steroids.
cases.answer: **Rickets** — vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D~3~ is formed in the skin when the B ring of 7-dehydrocholesterol is opened by UVB light; in winter there is little sunlight, and breast milk contains little vitamin D. D~3~ is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and in the kidney to active **calcitriol**; calcitriol ensures the absorption of Ca^2+^ and phosphate in the intestine. When it is deficient, bone mineralization is disturbed. Treatment and prevention: vitamin D preparations, sunbathing, better nutrition.
